Rendering list starts/overrides, the separate Markdown list reader, endnote starts and page-number starts all preserve high document-controlled counter values and reach this common formatter. Existing alphabetic/Roman label limits do not protect Chicago labels.

finding.remediation: Enforce a shared maximum label length before repetition, using checked byte-size arithmetic. Apply a documented bounded Chicago counter policy or typed refusal so all reading, page, note and list consumers share the same protection.

counterEvidence: The Markdown reader clamps nesting to eight but does not cap the counter's start magnitude.
Other formats have bounded Roman/alphabetic policies; Chicago's constructor lacks them.
Archive and XML budgets constrain the tiny source representation, not its label expansion.
Host CPU/memory limits can contain worker failure.
limitations: No allocation trigger executed; shared-service deployment is not established.

finding.title: Chicago numbering turns short start values into gigabytes of text
finding.summary: The shared Chicago numbering formatter repeats a symbol in proportion to an untrusted numeric start. A DOCX list start or override, endnote start, or page start can reach this formatter without an output-length budget; the Markdown reader also calls it. A short numeric attribute can cause a multi-gigabyte label allocation.

severity.rationale: Attacker-controlled documents can exhaust or terminate their reading/rendering process. No shared service or wider compromise is assumed.
severity.changeConditions: A bounded formatter/output budget removes the issue; per-request process resource isolation limits impact.

confidence.rationale: Parent verified the shared repeat sink, parsing and calls from rendering lists/endnotes/pages and Markdown list labels. No runtime allocation test was executed.

rootCause.summary: List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.

previousFindings.remediation: Bound generated byte/glyph length inside the shared Chicago formatter before repetition, with a documented safe cycle/fallback or typed refusal. Apply that bound to all list, startOverride, section-page and Markdown/direct list_number callers; do not rely on input bytes, counter saturation or later clipping.

counterEvidence: Other alphabetic and Roman formats have explicit wrapping maxima, but Chicago has no corresponding bound (convert/mod.rs:6492-6520).
Admission constrains input bytes and depth; it does not constrain generated label length.
Counter saturation prevents integer overflow but preserves enormous values.

Admission restricts input bytes and XML structure, not the expanded label. Sibling alphabetic and Roman formatters explicitly cycle at ALPHA_LABEL_MAX and ROMAN_LABEL_MAX (lines 6491-6514); Chicago lacks an equivalent bound.
Host process resource limits can contain failure but do not bound the allocation request.

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): Numbering levels accept an uncapped u32 start and the counter renderer passes it to format_num. The Chicago formatter repeats its selected symbol n/4 times without a label-length budget. Page numbering and the DOCX-to-Markdown list view call the same formatter, so the same missing control affects distinct consumers.

previousFindings.remediation: Bound generated byte/glyph length inside the shared Chicago formatter before repetition, with a documented safe cycle/fallback or typed refusal. Apply that bound to all list, startOverride, section-page and Markdown/direct list_number callers; do not rely on input bytes, counter saturation or later clipping.

counterEvidence: Other alphabetic and Roman formats have explicit wrapping maxima, but Chicago has no corresponding bound (convert/mod.rs:6492-6520).
Admission constrains input bytes and depth; it does not constrain generated label length.
Counter saturation prevents integer overflow but preserves enormous values.

Admission restricts input bytes and XML structure, not the expanded label. Sibling alphabetic and Roman formatters explicitly cycle at ALPHA_LABEL_MAX and ROMAN_LABEL_MAX (lines 6491-6514); Chicago lacks an equivalent bound.
Host process resource limits can contain failure but do not bound the allocation request.
Alphabetic labels wrap at ALPHA_LABEL_MAX=780 and Roman labels at 32767; those related claims are rejected.
The attack uses level zero, so it does not require the separate high-ilvl issue.
Archive/input bounds do not bound generated marker length.
Other numbering formats use bounded representations or wrapping; that does not constrain Chicago's String::repeat.
A process/WASM memory ceiling may terminate or reject the allocation but does not produce the expected typed input refusal.
Saturating counter increments prevent arithmetic wrap but do not cap marker size.
The attack works at normal level zero, so enforcing the supported level range does not fix it.
Input byte/depth/attribute limits do not cap the magnitude of the small numeric start.
An agent-view counter uses the shared formatter and likewise needs the output-length bound.

validation.summary:
The validated traces establish full-u32 list/startOverride propagation and independent section-page and Markdown numbered-list callers. A level with chicago, lvlText %1 and start 4294967295 yields 1073741824 repetitions of a three-byte symbol, requesting 3 GiB before shaping/copying. Section labels are evaluated on ordinary paragraphs even without bookmarks. Alphabetic/Roman siblings cycle at explicit maxima; Chicago does not. Source XML remains small and shallow.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Independently traced DOCX w:lvl/w:start -> NumLevel.start -> next_marker/render -> format_num(Chicago) -> chicago_label::repeat; Markdown list labels call the shared list_number formatter.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): For n=4294967295, chicago_label computes i=4294967294 and repeats the three-byte double-dagger symbol 1073741824 times, requesting 3221225472 bytes before additional copies. A normal numbered paragraph with numFmt=chicago and lvlText=%1 reaches the list renderer. pgNumType/@start with fmt=chicago reaches the page-label branch, and Markdown list_marker delegates to list_number. ZIP/XML depth/byte bounds do not constrain the numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed start 4,294,967,295 at normal ilvl=0 selects the three-byte double-dagger marker repeated 1,073,741,824 times: 3,221,225,472 requested output bytes. This is independent of excessive numbering levels.

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): Numbering levels accept an uncapped u32 start and the counter renderer passes it to format_num. The Chicago formatter repeats its selected symbol n/4 times without a label-length budget. Page numbering and the DOCX-to-Markdown list view call the same formatter, so the same missing control affects distinct consumers.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): Numbering start/startOverride values enter u32 counters with only max(1). `Numbering::render()` calls `format_num()`, whose Chicago branch repeats one marker `(n-1)/4+1` times without an output budget.

previousFindings.remediation: Bound generated byte/glyph length inside the shared Chicago formatter before repetition, with a documented safe cycle/fallback or typed refusal. Apply that bound to all list, startOverride, section-page and Markdown/direct list_number callers; do not rely on input bytes, counter saturation or later clipping.

A level with chicago, lvlText %1 and start 4294967295 yields 1073741824 repetitions of a three-byte symbol, requesting 3 GiB before shaping/copying. rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): Numbering levels accept an uncapped u32 start and the counter renderer passes it to format_num. The Chicago formatter repeats its selected symbol n/4 times without a label-length budget. Page numbering and the DOCX-to-Markdown list view call the same formatter, so the same missing control affects distinct consumers.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): Numbering start/startOverride values enter u32 counters with only max(1). `Numbering::render()` calls `format_num()`, whose Chicago branch repeats one marker `(n-1)/4+1` times without an output budget.
Endnote numStart/format also reaches the same shared formatter through number_endnote_refs; its generated-label budget must cover that route as well as list, page and agent/MCP read-view consumers.

previousFindings.remediation: Bound generated byte/glyph length inside the shared Chicago formatter before repetition, with a documented safe cycle/fallback or typed refusal. Apply that bound to all list, startOverride, section-page and Markdown/direct list_number callers; do not rely on input bytes, counter saturation or later clipping. Include authored endnote numStart/format and MCP agent-view callers in the shared formatter budget.

validation.summary:
The validated traces establish full-u32 list/startOverride propagation and independent section-page and Markdown numbered-list callers. A level with chicago, lvlText %1 and start 4294967295 yields 1073741824 repetitions of a three-byte symbol, requesting 3 GiB before shaping/copying. Section labels are evaluated on ordinary paragraphs even without bookmarks. Alphabetic/Roman siblings cycle at explicit maxima; Chicago does not. Source XML remains small and shallow.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Independently traced DOCX w:lvl/w:start -> NumLevel.start -> next_marker/render -> format_num(Chicago) -> chicago_label::repeat; Markdown list labels call the shared list_number formatter.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): For n=4294967295, chicago_label computes i=4294967294 and repeats the three-byte double-dagger symbol 1073741824 times, requesting 3221225472 bytes before additional copies. A normal numbered paragraph with numFmt=chicago and lvlText=%1 reaches the list renderer. pgNumType/@start with fmt=chicago reaches the page-label branch, and Markdown list_marker delegates to list_number. ZIP/XML depth/byte bounds do not constrain the numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed start 4,294,967,295 at normal ilvl=0 selects the three-byte double-dagger marker repeated 1,073,741,824 times: 3,221,225,472 requested output bytes. This is independent of excessive numbering levels.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Verified initial counter selection, render formatting and repeat arithmetic. A start of 4294967295 selects the double-dagger marker and requests 3,221,225,472 UTF-8 bytes. XML size and depth remain small; source byte limits cannot prevent the allocation.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): For n=2147483647, i=n-1=2147483646; i%4=2 selects the three-byte double dagger, and i/4+1=536870912 produces 1610612736 bytes before copies. List starts, startOverride, reader starts, endnote numStart and page pgNumType.start are parsed without a maximum. Both Numbering::render and the agent reader call the shared formatter. The native read_view adapter calls markdown::read (jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:899-901).

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): Numbering levels accept an uncapped u32 start and the counter renderer passes it to format_num. The Chicago formatter repeats its selected symbol n/4 times without a label-length budget. Page numbering and the DOCX-to-Markdown list view call the same formatter, so the same missing control affects distinct consumers.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): Numbering start/startOverride values enter u32 counters with only max(1). `Numbering::render()` calls `format_num()`, whose Chicago branch repeats one marker `(n-1)/4+1` times without an output budget.
Endnote numStart/format also reaches the same shared formatter through number_endnote_refs; its generated-label budget must cover that route as well as list, page and agent/MCP read-view consumers.
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: A shared formatter converts a bounded-width but numerically huge input into output proportional to its magnitude, without checking the resulting label length before String::repeat.

previousFindings.remediation: Bound generated byte/glyph length inside the shared Chicago formatter before repetition, with a documented safe cycle/fallback or typed refusal. Apply that bound to all list, startOverride, section-page and Markdown/direct list_number callers; do not rely on input bytes, counter saturation or later clipping. Include authored endnote numStart/format and MCP agent-view callers in the shared formatter budget.

validation.summary:
The validated traces establish full-u32 list/startOverride propagation and independent section-page and Markdown numbered-list callers. A level with chicago, lvlText %1 and start 4294967295 yields 1073741824 repetitions of a three-byte symbol, requesting 3 GiB before shaping/copying. Section labels are evaluated on ordinary paragraphs even without bookmarks. Alphabetic/Roman siblings cycle at explicit maxima; Chicago does not. Source XML remains small and shallow.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Independently traced DOCX w:lvl/w:start -> NumLevel.start -> next_marker/render -> format_num(Chicago) -> chicago_label::repeat; Markdown list labels call the shared list_number formatter.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): For n=4294967295, chicago_label computes i=4294967294 and repeats the three-byte double-dagger symbol 1073741824 times, requesting 3221225472 bytes before additional copies. A normal numbered paragraph with numFmt=chicago and lvlText=%1 reaches the list renderer. pgNumType/@start with fmt=chicago reaches the page-label branch, and Markdown list_marker delegates to list_number. ZIP/XML depth/byte bounds do not constrain the numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed start 4,294,967,295 at normal ilvl=0 selects the three-byte double-dagger marker repeated 1,073,741,824 times: 3,221,225,472 requested output bytes. This is independent of excessive numbering levels.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Verified initial counter selection, render formatting and repeat arithmetic. A start of 4294967295 selects the double-dagger marker and requests 3,221,225,472 UTF-8 bytes. XML size and depth remain small; source byte limits cannot prevent the allocation.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): For n=2147483647, i=n-1=2147483646; i%4=2 selects the three-byte double dagger, and i/4+1=536870912 produces 1610612736 bytes before copies. List starts, startOverride, reader starts, endnote numStart and page pgNumType.start are parsed without a maximum. Both Numbering::render and the agent reader call the shared formatter. The native read_view adapter calls markdown::read (jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:899-901).
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: Parent verified all reported callers of format_num/chicago_label. Rendering list and startOverride, page numbering and endnote numbering accept attacker u32 values; Markdown passes parsed starts/overrides to the same formatter. This is distinct from oversized list-level iteration: even ordinary level zero reaches it.

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): Numbering levels accept an uncapped u32 start and the counter renderer passes it to format_num. The Chicago formatter repeats its selected symbol n/4 times without a label-length budget. Page numbering and the DOCX-to-Markdown list view call the same formatter, so the same missing control affects distinct consumers.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): Numbering start/startOverride values enter u32 counters with only max(1). `Numbering::render()` calls `format_num()`, whose Chicago branch repeats one marker `(n-1)/4+1` times without an output budget.
Endnote numStart/format also reaches the same shared formatter through number_endnote_refs; its generated-label budget must cover that route as well as list, page and agent/MCP read-view consumers.
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: A shared formatter converts a bounded-width but numerically huge input into output proportional to its magnitude, without checking the resulting label length before String::repeat.

previousFindings.remediation: Bound generated byte/glyph length inside the shared Chicago formatter before repetition, with a documented safe cycle/fallback or typed refusal. Apply that bound to all list, startOverride, section-page and Markdown/direct list_number callers; do not rely on input bytes, counter saturation or later clipping. Include authored endnote numStart/format and MCP agent-view callers in the shared formatter budget.

validation.summary:
The validated traces establish full-u32 list/startOverride propagation and independent section-page and Markdown numbered-list callers. A level with chicago, lvlText %1 and start 4294967295 yields 1073741824 repetitions of a three-byte symbol, requesting 3 GiB before shaping/copying. Section labels are evaluated on ordinary paragraphs even without bookmarks. Alphabetic/Roman siblings cycle at explicit maxima; Chicago does not. Source XML remains small and shallow.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Independently traced DOCX w:lvl/w:start -> NumLevel.start -> next_marker/render -> format_num(Chicago) -> chicago_label::repeat; Markdown list labels call the shared list_number formatter.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): For n=4294967295, chicago_label computes i=4294967294 and repeats the three-byte double-dagger symbol 1073741824 times, requesting 3221225472 bytes before additional copies. A normal numbered paragraph with numFmt=chicago and lvlText=%1 reaches the list renderer. pgNumType/@start with fmt=chicago reaches the page-label branch, and Markdown list_marker delegates to list_number. ZIP/XML depth/byte bounds do not constrain the numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed start 4,294,967,295 at normal ilvl=0 selects the three-byte double-dagger marker repeated 1,073,741,824 times: 3,221,225,472 requested output bytes. This is independent of excessive numbering levels.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Verified initial counter selection, render formatting and repeat arithmetic. A start of 4294967295 selects the double-dagger marker and requests 3,221,225,472 UTF-8 bytes. XML size and depth remain small; source byte limits cannot prevent the allocation.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): For n=2147483647, i=n-1=2147483646; i%4=2 selects the three-byte double dagger, and i/4+1=536870912 produces 1610612736 bytes before copies. List starts, startOverride, reader starts, endnote numStart and page pgNumType.start are parsed without a maximum. Both Numbering::render and the agent reader call the shared formatter. The native read_view adapter calls markdown::read (jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:899-901).
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: Parent verified all reported callers of format_num/chicago_label. Rendering list and startOverride, page numbering and endnote numbering accept attacker u32 values; Markdown passes parsed starts/overrides to the same formatter. This is distinct from oversized list-level iteration: even ordinary level zero reaches it.

findings.title: Rendering an HTML chunk can allocate gigabytes from a single colspan value
findings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory. The supplied positive 4294967295 framing fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and needs no arithmetic overflow.

severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.
severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.

confidence.rationale: Both independent baseline and focused investigator identified the mechanism; parent verified input parsing, post-admission expansion and allocation loop statically. No runtime reproduction was executed.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.

Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. finding.title: Converting an HTML altChunk can allocate billions of table columns
finding.summary: A small DOCX containing an HTML altChunk with a huge numeric `colspan` can exhaust memory or CPU during conversion. The importer accepts the value as `usize` and generates one `<w:gridCol>` per column before any layout or raster limit applies.

severity.rationale: A document supplier can trigger excessive allocation through the public conversion API with a small input and no configuration changes. Availability of the host process or WASM instance is affected; no remote service deployment, code execution or data theft is established. External process limits constrain collateral impact.
severity.changeConditions: A shared upload-processing process increases impact; bounded table columns and a checked expansion budget remove the amplification.

confidence.rationale: Parent source review confirms direct numeric parsing, table-close dispatch, unbounded output loop, and public conversion reachability; no application execution.

taxonomy.category: Unbounded allocation from HTML numeric input

codeEvidence.label: conversion public
codeEvidence.explanation: Caller-provided DOCX bytes enter public PDF conversion and reach with_pages/with_layout.

codeEvidence.label: conversion layout
codeEvidence.explanation: Admission happens before HTML expansion; the referenced chunk bytes are sent to altchunk::expand and resulting XML goes straight to a DOM.

codeEvidence.label: chunk repeat
codeEvidence.explanation: Each altChunk reference is loaded, decoded to HTML and converted by html_to_wml.

codeEvidence.label: html parser
codeEvidence.explanation: The HTML tokenizer dispatches each td/th opening tag to Builder::start and table closes to end_table.

codeEvidence.label: span input
codeEvidence.explanation: The colspan string is parsed into an unrestricted usize and retained on the cell stack.

codeEvidence.label: span count
codeEvidence.explanation: end_table sums cell spans into the table's column count without a cap.

codeEvidence.label: span output
codeEvidence.explanation: The column count controls one allocated XML grid-column string per iteration.

rootCause.summary: `Builder::start` treats `colspan` as any positive usize. `end_cell` retains that span, and `end_table` sums it into `cols` before a `0..cols` loop materializes XML for every column. Package admission runs on the original DOCX and does not bound this derived HTML table size.

finding.remediation: Enforce a practical maximum cell span and checked per-row/total column counts before generating any table markup; charge all generated WML to an expansion budget and return a typed input-limit refusal.

counterEvidence: ZIP and XML budgets limit original package entries; they do not limit the numeric colspan or derived WML.
Page raster MAX_PAGE_PIXELS is reached later and does not constrain this importer.
limitations: No runtime reproduction or exact memory measurement; numeric allocation consequence follows directly from the loop.
validation.summary: Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.

dataflow.summary: DOCX bytes → with_layout admission → altChunk relationship load → HTML td colspan → cell span → end_table cols → per-column String growth.

impact.why: Loss of embedding process/instance availability.

likelihood.why: A small numeric HTML field directly determines work.

For example, a span of 1,000,000,000 entails a billion formatting iterations and tens of gigabytes of generated XML before DOM parsing, exhausting the rendering process.

severity.rationale: Process availability impact is medium and likelihood is high once an untrusted document is rendered: a tiny integer attribute drives immediate deterministic unbounded work. No remote service deployment is assumed.
severity.changeConditions: A shared conversion service increases operational impact. Strict external process memory/CPU limits contain host-wide impact but still allow the input to terminate its conversion worker.

confidence.rationale: Parent verified the admitted-byte entrypoint, internal relationship loading, usize parsing and per-column emission loop. No material source reachability blocker; no runtime payload executed.

codeEvidence.label: Expansion runs after original package admission

rootCause.summary: The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.

finding.remediation: Refuse out-of-range HTML column spans before adding cells; use checked cumulative grid accounting and a small documented maximum column count. limitations: No runtime reproduction or deployment-specific concurrency impact measured.

finding.title: Rendering an embedded HTML table can exhaust process memory
finding.summary: Rendering a small DOCX containing an HTML altChunk with a large `colspan` allocates one generated grid column per attacker-supplied span value. A single cell with `colspan="1000000000"` causes a billion string writes before layout, bypassing the original package's input-size budgets.

severity.rationale: A document author can deterministically exhaust CPU and memory in a consuming renderer with a tiny input. Availability impact is high for that process, but remote/shared-service deployment is not established and process limits can contain it.

confidence.rationale: Direct source trace establishes attacker-controlled integer parsing and the unbounded allocation loop after admission; no runtime exploit was executed.

taxonomy.category: Uncontrolled resource consumption during HTML expansion

codeEvidence.label: Admission precedes HTML expansion
codeEvidence.explanation: The renderer loads a relationship-targeted chunk from the admitted package and expands it before DOM layout; generated output has no size gate here.

codeEvidence.label: Chunk bytes become HTML and generated WML
codeEvidence.explanation: Attacker-authored HTML is converted locally into a new WML string; archive inflation bounds do not constrain this representation expansion.

codeEvidence.label: HTML colspan accepted without upper bound
codeEvidence.explanation: Any positive span fitting usize survives unchanged; the lower clamp adds no upper bound.

codeEvidence.label: Span values determine generated grid length
codeEvidence.code:
let cols = table
            .rows
            .iter()
            .map(|r| r.iter().map(|c| c.span).sum::<usize>())
            .max()
            .unwrap_or(1)
            .max(1);
        let col_w = 9360 / cols;
codeEvidence.explanation: A one-cell row sets cols directly to the supplied span, independently of input length.

codeEvidence.label: One string write for each column
codeEvidence.explanation: The attacker-sized loop grows the output string by tens of gigabytes for a billion-column cell before later validation could occur.

rootCause.summary: `with_layout()` admits the original DOCX, then `expand()` loads its HTML chunk and passes it to `html_to_wml()`. finding.remediation: Reject spans and total table column counts above a documented limit before construction; use checked addition and enforce a generated-output/work budget shared across all HTML chunks.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output.

previousFindings.remediation: Enforce a practical maximum cell span and checked per-row/aggregate column counts before generating any table XML. Charge all HTML/MHT-generated WML, including repeated/nested tables, to a cumulative byte/work budget inside altChunk expansion and return a typed input-limit refusal before allocation or DOM construction.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output.

previousFindings.remediation: Enforce a practical maximum cell span and checked per-row/aggregate column counts before generating any table XML. Charge all HTML/MHT-generated WML, including repeated/nested tables, to a cumulative byte/work budget inside altChunk expansion and return a typed input-limit refusal before allocation or DOM construction.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.

previousFindings.remediation: Enforce a practical maximum cell span and checked per-row/aggregate column counts before generating any table XML. Charge all HTML/MHT-generated WML, including repeated/nested tables, to a cumulative byte/work budget inside altChunk expansion and return a typed input-limit refusal before allocation or DOM construction.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.

rootCause.summary:
parse_tab_stops accepts arbitrary f32 pos values. The compatibility landing correction clamps only Right-aligned stops in mode>=15, leaving Left stops unchanged. advance_tab computes the authored destination, and paint_tab_leader casts its geometric mark count to usize and calls repeat before painting can clip output.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `parse_tab_stops()` retains an arbitrarily large floating position. Layout preserves left stops, and a lone explicit tab survives wrapping. `advance_tab()` passes its distant endpoint to `paint_tab_leader()`, which casts the calculated count to usize and repeats a marker.

findings.remediation: Reject nonfinite coordinates and cap tab destinations or generated leader glyphs to the visible line/page extent before constructing strings.

counterEvidence: Package admission does not bound numeric layout values. Right-stop compatibility clamping does not protect Left leaders. The eventual text clipping occurs after the allocation.
Host process resource limits can contain failure but do not bound the allocation request.
Admission bounds source ZIP/XML size, nesting and entries, and the policy recommends host process limits. These do not bound this generated work.
Modern right-aligned tab clamping does not cover the left-aligned trigger; raster pixel limits are downstream.

validation.summary:

This is independently reachable from grid and numbering findings.

rootCause.summary: The nesting guard tracks recursive parser calls. nested_list instead iteratively takes its previous output node as a new script base, preserving existing Scripts nodes through take_base. returnedFinding.title: Flat LaTeX script chains bypass the nesting guard and overflow the writer stack
returnedFinding.attacker: A party supplying Markdown converted through the public Markdown-to-DOCX API or corresponding CLI/binding.
returnedFinding.violated_security_invariant: The math nesting limit must bound the depth of the AST subsequently traversed and destroyed, including depth created by iterative wrapping.
returnedFinding.source_to_sink: For each superscript or subscript, nested_list removes the previous output node and wraps it in a new Node::Scripts. returnedFinding.concrete_impact: Markdown consisting of '$a' followed by roughly 100000 repetitions of '^1' and a closing '$' creates an approximately 100000-level AST from about 200 KB of input. Writing or dropping that tree can exhaust the native stack or trap the WASM instance.

findings.title: WMF record-boundary failures amplify polygon work and retained text
findings.summary: Rendering a DOCX with a crafted placeable WMF lets short declared records consume payload from later records, which the outer parser then revisits. Polygon/polypolygon/polyline records can cause billions of coordinate decodes from roughly 512 KiB; EXTTEXTOUT/TEXTOUT records can retain hundreds of megabytes of overlapping owned strings from roughly 205.6 KB. The common missing record-local boundary bypasses the canvas cap and original package budgets. A further framing uses alternating six-byte EXTTEXTOUT and unknown 0xFFFF record headers to claim 65,535 text bytes from subsequent records, implying several GiB of retained strings from roughly 1 MiB of media; this is a static estimate. A supplied 7-word EXTTEXTOUT framing uses 65536 fourteen-byte records plus a 65535-byte suffix in less than 1 MiB and requests about 4 GiB of decoded characters; nonzero mapping dimensions and nonblank text are required. This is a static estimate.

severity.rationale: Default document rendering can amplify a small embedded WMF into excessive coordinate/raster work or large retained text allocations, affecting host-process or WASM availability. Shared-host blast radius depends on caller process isolation; no memory-unsafe out-of-bounds read, disclosure or code execution is established.
severity.changeConditions: Mandatory record-local parsing and validated counts across all WMF handlers remove the overlapping-payload amplification; cumulative work/text budgets and isolated workers constrain resource effects.

confidence.rationale: Independent worker and parent verified the concrete input-to-sink control failure statically; exact runtime resource/failure thresholds were not measured.

rootCause.summary:
raster_wmf checks declared size*2 against remaining file bytes but keeps passing the entire data slice to its handlers, then advances only by the declared record size. Polygon, polypolygon and polyline counts therefore cause coordinate reads/allocation/raster work across later records. Independently, META_EXTTEXTOUT/META_TEXTOUT counts slice later bytes as text; wmf_text decodes owned Strings retained in texts and ultimately ImageKind::Metafile. Both subcases repeatedly consume overlapping suffixes because consumed payload extent is not tied to outer advancement. EMF's analogous point helper checks off+size. A mandatory record-limited slice plus record-local field/count checks at this shared WMF dispatch boundary fixes all absorbed handlers; geometry-only count patches leave text retention reachable.
With size=3 the outer cursor advances six bytes. EXTTEXTOUT's count at payload+4 can come from the next unknown-0xFFFF header; options may select a later optional-rectangle string offset. Subsequent header bytes repeatedly supply large whole-file text spans. Both drawing and VML image relationships reach this decoder before the general image crate's default 512 MiB allocation limit, which therefore cannot bound this earlier retention. The supplied alternating-header proof gives options=3, selecting the optional-rectangle branch and a string start at payload+16.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): WMF variable-length record data is read against the whole input rather than the record's declared slice; declared record progression permits overlapping unbounded amplification. A seven-word EXTTEXTOUT record contains its six-byte header and eight-byte fixed fields but can start its 65535-byte text range at the next record, because only whole-file bounds are checked.
Assigned discovery-0016 adds a same-function-header proof: repeated six-byte size=3/0x0A32 headers cause count at off+10 to read the next function (2610), options at off+12 to read size (3), and optional-rectangle text to start at off+22. Nonzero mapping extents, nonblank bytes and sufficient trailing data retain overlapping Strings; roughly 6 MB of records request about 2.6 GB of strings. These are source-derived estimates.
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: Text record handlers do not constrain field/string reads to the declared record extent, allowing small records to repeatedly materialize overlapping bytes as owned strings.

findings.remediation: Confine every WMF handler, including field, font, string and geometry reads, to a slice limited to its checked declared record extent. Before allocation validate fixed fields, ring/point counts and coordinate arrays, EXTTEXTOUT options/optional rectangle and text count, and TEXTOUT padded string plus trailing coordinates against that slice using checked arithmetic. Refuse inconsistent records before decoding/rasterization/replay and enforce cumulative decoded-text, record and total geometry/work budgets. Keep the already bounded EMF behavior.

Parent independently read raster_wmf dispatch/record checks and all three polygon handlers, their file-wide reads and outer offset increment. Repeated eight-byte polygon records with point-count 65535 can repeatedly consume later record bytes as coordinate payload; a 512KiB file supports more than two billion decodes before a late truncation refusal. This is bounded by whole-file bytes rather than record bytes; no memory out-of-bounds access is claimed.
Verified that text counts are u16, checked against the entire buffer, and do not need to fit the declared record. A 14-byte EXTTEXTOUT record can claim 65,535 text bytes beyond its own end. Ten thousand such records with enough trailing bytes imply 655,350,000 source bytes decoded into retained Strings from about 205.6 KB of WMF; UTF-8 conversion and later text handling can add cost.

Tens of thousands of such records in roughly 1 MB imply several GB of overlapping decoded text. This is an estimate from the supplied source, not executed memory measurement; ordinary bounds, nonblank content and sufficient trailing data are prerequisites.

Assigned discovery-0007 corroboration (preserved Standard static validation; no reducer verification): Verified the record cursor at metafile.rs:684 advances by size2 while handlers at 603-620 read against data. Approximately 65536 14-byte records plus 65535 trailing bytes fit in ~1 MiB yet retain at least ~4 GiB of text. WMF detection checks the placeable magic; bounded canvas dimensions do not bound text. Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Parent inspected WMF dispatch, header/canvas setup, complete record loop (445-687), ansi_text (430-442) and wmf_text retention (692-716). Repeated eight-byte TEXTOUT records (4 words) can each declare 65535 bytes, with coordinates and tail inside the overall file and an EOF before unused tail; nonzero extents and nonblank bytes satisfy retention. EXTTEXTOUT and all three point-array opcodes share the boundary failure.
Additional assigned static framing: roughly 100000 eight-byte TEXTOUT records each claiming 65535 bytes plus sufficient trailing bytes (EOF before unused tail) fit in roughly 1 MiB and imply several GiB of overlapping retained strings. finding.title: Rendering malformed WMF text records can exhaust memory
finding.summary: The WMF parser checks a record's outer extent but reads its text fields against the entire file. Repeated six-byte EXTTEXTOUT records can each copy thousands of overlapping bytes from later records into retained strings, expanding a few megabytes of embedded media into gigabytes.

severity.rationale: Attacker-authored embedded WMF can exhaust a rendering process; downstream service exposure and collateral damage depend on deployment isolation.

confidence.rationale: Independent source and offset arithmetic verify the zero-payload record acceptance, subsequent-record reads and retained text copies.

codeEvidence.explanation: size=3 permits a six-byte header with zero payload; later readers still receive the entire file.

codeEvidence.label: Text fields and ranges use whole-file bounds

codeEvidence.label: Copied strings retained as MetaText
codeEvidence.explanation: ansi_text owns a fresh String for each record; texts.extend retains it until parsing completes, multiplying overlapping bytes.

rootCause.summary: `decode_image()` routes embedded WMF bytes to `raster_wmf()`. Its outer loop accepts any size of at least three 16-bit words and checks only that this extent fits the remaining file. EXTTEXTOUT and TEXTOUT then read fields and text using the whole data slice. A malformed short record borrows count/text bytes from following records; `wmf_text()` allocates a new String and the parser retains every result. Advancing by the declared six bytes allows the same input ranges to be copied hundreds of times.

finding.remediation: Slice each WMF record to its declared extent before reading any field; validate minimum payloads and count-derived ranges within that slice for text/font/polygon and other sibling records. Add an aggregate extracted-text/work budget.

counterEvidence: Checked multiplication bounds outer offset progression; this is not an out-of-buffer read.
Canvas dimensions are capped at 384, but text storage is separate.
ZIP admission bounds original media bytes, not overlapping text-copy work.
limitations: No malformed input or application code was executed.

validation.summary: Parent verified repeated little-endian size=3/function=0x0A32 headers: count at off+10 reads next function (2610), options at off+12 reads following size (3), and text starts at off+22. With nonzero placeable extents and sufficient trailing bytes, every six-byte record retains about 2610 bytes. Roughly 6 MB records request about 2.6 GB strings.

rootCause.summary: Text record handlers do not constrain field/string reads to the declared record extent, allowing small records to repeatedly materialize overlapping bytes as owned strings.

finding.remediation: Slice every WMF record to its validated declared extent and decode all fields, optional rectangles, strings and padding exclusively within that slice. Refuse undersized records. Bound aggregate decoded text and record counts independently of raster dimensions.

rootCause.summary: The WMF outer loop validates only that declared record size fits remaining file bytes, then passes the entire data slice to handlers. Polygon, polypolygon and polyline counts drive loops that use file-bounded reads rather than the current record extent. The outer loop still advances only by declared size, so the same following bytes can be decoded as points again for each short record. EMF's analogous point helper correctly checks against off+size.

previousFindings.remediation: Confine each WMF handler to its declared record slice; validate ring and point counts against that slice with checked arithmetic before allocation/rasterization, and bound total parser work.

rootCause.summary:
raster_wmf checks declared size*2 against remaining file bytes but keeps passing the entire data slice to its handlers, then advances only by the declared record size. Polygon, polypolygon and polyline counts therefore cause coordinate reads/allocation/raster work across later records. Independently, META_EXTTEXTOUT/META_TEXTOUT counts slice later bytes as text; wmf_text decodes owned Strings retained in texts and ultimately ImageKind::Metafile. Both subcases repeatedly consume overlapping suffixes because consumed payload extent is not tied to outer advancement. EMF's analogous point helper checks off+size. A mandatory record-limited slice plus record-local field/count checks at this shared WMF dispatch boundary fixes all absorbed handlers; geometry-only count patches leave text retention reachable.
With size=3 the outer cursor advances six bytes. EXTTEXTOUT's count at payload+4 can come from the next unknown-0xFFFF header; options may select a later optional-rectangle string offset. Subsequent header bytes repeatedly supply large whole-file text spans. Both drawing and VML image relationships reach this decoder before the general image crate's default 512 MiB allocation limit, which therefore cannot bound this earlier retention. The supplied alternating-header proof gives options=3, selecting the optional-rectangle branch and a string start at payload+16.

previousFindings.remediation: Confine every WMF handler, including field, font, string and geometry reads, to a slice limited to its checked declared record extent. Before allocation validate fixed fields, ring/point counts and coordinate arrays, EXTTEXTOUT options/optional rectangle and text count, and TEXTOUT padded string plus trailing coordinates against that slice using checked arithmetic. Refuse inconsistent records before decoding/rasterization/replay and enforce cumulative decoded-text, record and total geometry/work budgets. Keep the already bounded EMF behavior.

validation.summary:
Parent independently read raster_wmf dispatch/record checks and all three polygon handlers, their file-wide reads and outer offset increment. Repeated eight-byte polygon records with point-count 65535 can repeatedly consume later record bytes as coordinate payload; a 512KiB file supports more than two billion decodes before a late truncation refusal. This is bounded by whole-file bytes rather than record bytes; no memory out-of-bounds access is claimed.
Verified that text counts are u16, checked against the entire buffer, and do not need to fit the declared record. A 14-byte EXTTEXTOUT record can claim 65,535 text bytes beyond its own end. Ten thousand such records with enough trailing bytes imply 655,350,000 source bytes decoded into retained Strings from about 205.6 KB of WMF; UTF-8 conversion and later text handling can add cost.
Additional static proof: a placeable WMF with nonzero mapping bounds and fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT records (y/x/count/options, options zero, n=65535, no record-local text) reads following records into retained strings. Tens of thousands of such records in roughly 1 MB imply several GB of overlapping decoded text. This is an estimate from the supplied source, not executed memory measurement; ordinary bounds, nonblank content and sufficient trailing data are prerequisites.
Assigned discovery-0010 Standard corroboration (source validation, not reducer verification): Parent confirmed size3 advances6 bytes, EXTTEXTOUT reads count at payload+4, string at payload+8/16 and checks only data.get(at..at+n). Alternating six-byte EXTTEXTOUT/unknown0xFFFF headers supply count65535 from the next header while allowing repeated advancement. ansi_text collects owned strings retained in texts. TEXTOUT shares the record-local bounds omission.

extensions.semanticReductionNotes:
The supplied static proof framing uses repeated eight-byte WMF polygon records with count 65535. In a roughly 512 KiB file, the first roughly 32768 records can each decode following-record bytes as 65535 points, exceeding two billion decodes plus polygon scans before late truncation refusal. META_POLYGON, META_POLYPOLYGON and META_POLYLINE all need record-local bounds; the 384-pixel canvas cap, whole-file safe reads and bounded EMF helper do not enforce those WMF record bounds.
dedup-0003 merges the same shared WMF record-slice violation, rather than a mere media/sink family match. Preserve both proof tuples and all five handlers: eight-byte polygon records with count 65535 in ~512 KiB yield >2 billion point decodes; 10000 fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT records claiming 65535 bytes with sufficient nonblank following data yield 655350000 source bytes decoded into retained Strings from ~205.6 KB. Text records need nonblank decoded content and valid ordinary mapping to retain MetaText; EXTTEXTOUT rectangle/options and TEXTOUT padding/coordinate layouts require record-local checks. The text source independently validates its text consequences, while previous validated evidence establishes geometry consequences. Actual failure thresholds remain unmeasured. The common remediation limits the slice at dispatch for every handler; fixing only polygon handlers would not subsume the text source. MAX_SIDE=384, object-count clamps and safe whole-file reads remain useful but do not limit these repeated payloads.
dedup-0005: Same raster_wmf record extent versus whole-file handler access. Mandatory checked record slices across all field/string/font/geometry handlers subsume the assigned text and geometry report; a geometry-only patch would not. The assigned proof uses nonzero placeable bounds, fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT y/x/count/options headers with options=0 and n=65535, no local text, and tens of thousands of records in roughly 1 MB to retain several GB of overlapping decoded strings. This supplements, rather than replaces, the prior 10,000-record/~205.6 KB text and ~512 KiB polygon proofs. Preserve nonblank/mapping prerequisites, size>=3 words/advancing cursor, canvas clipping, whole-file memory safety and absent runtime measurements.
dedup-0008: The same WMF dispatch-wide missing record-local boundary; the retained mandatory record slice and field/count checks subsume the six-byte size=3 alternating EXTTEXTOUT/unknown-0xFFFF framing, including VML image callers. Preserve prior polygon, polyline, polypolygon, fourteen-byte text and TEXTOUT proofs, new several-GiB estimate and options/rectangle nuance. Geometry-only or one-text-handler-only repairs are insufficient; no runtime memory measurement or memory-unsafe access is asserted.

extensions.semanticReductionNotes:
The supplied static proof framing uses repeated eight-byte WMF polygon records with count 65535. In a roughly 512 KiB file, the first roughly 32768 records can each decode following-record bytes as 65535 points, exceeding two billion decodes plus polygon scans before late truncation refusal. META_POLYGON, META_POLYPOLYGON and META_POLYLINE all need record-local bounds; the 384-pixel canvas cap, whole-file safe reads and bounded EMF helper do not enforce those WMF record bounds.
dedup-0003 merges the same shared WMF record-slice violation, rather than a mere media/sink family match. Preserve both proof tuples and all five handlers: eight-byte polygon records with count 65535 in ~512 KiB yield >2 billion point decodes; 10000 fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT records claiming 65535 bytes with sufficient nonblank following data yield 655350000 source bytes decoded into retained Strings from ~205.6 KB. The text source independently validates its text consequences, while previous validated evidence establishes geometry consequences. Actual failure thresholds remain unmeasured. This supplements, rather than replaces, the prior 10,000-record/~205.6 KB text and ~512 KiB polygon proofs. dedup-0008: The same WMF dispatch-wide missing record-local boundary; the retained mandatory record slice and field/count checks subsume the six-byte size=3 alternating EXTTEXTOUT/unknown-0xFFFF framing, including VML image callers. previousFindings.title: WMF record-boundary failures amplify polygon work and retained text
previousFindings.summary: Rendering a DOCX with a crafted placeable WMF lets short declared records consume payload from later records, which the outer parser then revisits. Polygon/polypolygon/polyline records can cause billions of coordinate decodes from roughly 512 KiB; EXTTEXTOUT/TEXTOUT records can retain hundreds of megabytes of overlapping owned strings from roughly 205.6 KB. The common missing record-local boundary bypasses the canvas cap and original package budgets. A further framing uses alternating six-byte EXTTEXTOUT and unknown 0xFFFF record headers to claim 65,535 text bytes from subsequent records, implying several GiB of retained strings from roughly 1 MiB of media; this is a static estimate.

severity.rationale: Default document rendering can amplify a small embedded WMF into excessive coordinate/raster work or large retained text allocations, affecting host-process or WASM availability. Shared-host blast radius depends on caller process isolation; no memory-unsafe out-of-bounds read, disclosure or code execution is established.
severity.changeConditions: Mandatory record-local parsing and validated counts across all WMF handlers remove the overlapping-payload amplification; cumulative work/text budgets and isolated workers constrain resource effects.

confidence.rationale: Independent worker and parent verified the concrete input-to-sink control failure statically; exact runtime resource/failure thresholds were not measured.

rootCause.summary:
raster_wmf checks declared size*2 against remaining file bytes but keeps passing the entire data slice to its handlers, then advances only by the declared record size. Polygon, polypolygon and polyline counts therefore cause coordinate reads/allocation/raster work across later records. Independently, META_EXTTEXTOUT/META_TEXTOUT counts slice later bytes as text; wmf_text decodes owned Strings retained in texts and ultimately ImageKind::Metafile. Both subcases repeatedly consume overlapping suffixes because consumed payload extent is not tied to outer advancement. EMF's analogous point helper checks off+size. A mandatory record-limited slice plus record-local field/count checks at this shared WMF dispatch boundary fixes all absorbed handlers; geometry-only count patches leave text retention reachable.
With size=3 the outer cursor advances six bytes. EXTTEXTOUT's count at payload+4 can come from the next unknown-0xFFFF header; options may select a later optional-rectangle string offset. Subsequent header bytes repeatedly supply large whole-file text spans. Both drawing and VML image relationships reach this decoder before the general image crate's default 512 MiB allocation limit, which therefore cannot bound this earlier retention. The supplied alternating-header proof gives options=3, selecting the optional-rectangle branch and a string start at payload+16.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): WMF variable-length record data is read against the whole input rather than the record's declared slice; declared record progression permits overlapping unbounded amplification.

previousFindings.remediation: Confine every WMF handler, including field, font, string and geometry reads, to a slice limited to its checked declared record extent. Before allocation validate fixed fields, ring/point counts and coordinate arrays, EXTTEXTOUT options/optional rectangle and text count, and TEXTOUT padded string plus trailing coordinates against that slice using checked arithmetic. Refuse inconsistent records before decoding/rasterization/replay and enforce cumulative decoded-text, record and total geometry/work budgets. Keep the already bounded EMF behavior.

validation.summary:
Parent independently read raster_wmf dispatch/record checks and all three polygon handlers, their file-wide reads and outer offset increment. Repeated eight-byte polygon records with point-count 65535 can repeatedly consume later record bytes as coordinate payload; a 512KiB file supports more than two billion decodes before a late truncation refusal. This is bounded by whole-file bytes rather than record bytes; no memory out-of-bounds access is claimed.
Verified that text counts are u16, checked against the entire buffer, and do not need to fit the declared record. A 14-byte EXTTEXTOUT record can claim 65,535 text bytes beyond its own end. Ten thousand such records with enough trailing bytes imply 655,350,000 source bytes decoded into retained Strings from about 205.6 KB of WMF; UTF-8 conversion and later text handling can add cost.
Additional static proof: a placeable WMF with nonzero mapping bounds and fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT records (y/x/count/options, options zero, n=65535, no record-local text) reads following records into retained strings. Tens of thousands of such records in roughly 1 MB imply several GB of overlapping decoded text. This is an estimate from the supplied source, not executed memory measurement; ordinary bounds, nonblank content and sufficient trailing data are prerequisites.
Assigned discovery-0010 Standard corroboration (source validation, not reducer verification): Parent confirmed size3 advances6 bytes, EXTTEXTOUT reads count at payload+4, string at payload+8/16 and checks only data.get(at..at+n). Alternating six-byte EXTTEXTOUT/unknown0xFFFF headers supply count65535 from the next header while allowing repeated advancement. ansi_text collects owned strings retained in texts. TEXTOUT shares the record-local bounds omission.
Assigned discovery-0007 corroboration (preserved Standard static validation; no reducer verification): Verified the record cursor at metafile.rs:684 advances by size2 while handlers at 603-620 read against data. Approximately 65536 14-byte records plus 65535 trailing bytes fit in ~1 MiB yet retain at least ~4 GiB of text. WMF detection checks the placeable magic; bounded canvas dimensions do not bound text. Package admission permits such small binary media.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Parent inspected WMF dispatch, header/canvas setup, complete record loop (445-687), ansi_text (430-442) and wmf_text retention (692-716). Repeated eight-byte TEXTOUT records (4 words) can each declare 65535 bytes, with coordinates and tail inside the overall file and an EOF before unused tail; nonzero extents and nonblank bytes satisfy retention. EXTTEXTOUT and all three point-array opcodes share the boundary failure.
Additional assigned static framing: roughly 100000 eight-byte TEXTOUT records each claiming 65535 bytes plus sufficient trailing bytes (EOF before unused tail) fit in roughly 1 MiB and imply several GiB of overlapping retained strings. Nonzero mapping extents and nonblank decoded text are required. Matching short POLYGON/POLYLINE counts imply billions of point iterations. No payload or measurement was executed.

previousFindings.title: WMF record-boundary failures amplify polygon work and retained text
previousFindings.summary: Rendering a DOCX with a crafted placeable WMF lets short declared records consume payload from later records, which the outer parser then revisits. Polygon/polypolygon/polyline records can cause billions of coordinate decodes from roughly 512 KiB; EXTTEXTOUT/TEXTOUT records can retain hundreds of megabytes of overlapping owned strings from roughly 205.6 KB. The common missing record-local boundary bypasses the canvas cap and original package budgets. A further framing uses alternating six-byte EXTTEXTOUT and unknown 0xFFFF record headers to claim 65,535 text bytes from subsequent records, implying several GiB of retained strings from roughly 1 MiB of media; this is a static estimate.

severity.rationale: Default document rendering can amplify a small embedded WMF into excessive coordinate/raster work or large retained text allocations, affecting host-process or WASM availability. Shared-host blast radius depends on caller process isolation; no memory-unsafe out-of-bounds read, disclosure or code execution is established.
severity.changeConditions: Mandatory record-local parsing and validated counts across all WMF handlers remove the overlapping-payload amplification; cumulative work/text budgets and isolated workers constrain resource effects.

confidence.rationale: Independent worker and parent verified the concrete input-to-sink control failure statically; exact runtime resource/failure thresholds were not measured.

rootCause.summary:
raster_wmf checks declared size*2 against remaining file bytes but keeps passing the entire data slice to its handlers, then advances only by the declared record size. Polygon, polypolygon and polyline counts therefore cause coordinate reads/allocation/raster work across later records. Independently, META_EXTTEXTOUT/META_TEXTOUT counts slice later bytes as text; wmf_text decodes owned Strings retained in texts and ultimately ImageKind::Metafile. Both subcases repeatedly consume overlapping suffixes because consumed payload extent is not tied to outer advancement. EMF's analogous point helper checks off+size. A mandatory record-limited slice plus record-local field/count checks at this shared WMF dispatch boundary fixes all absorbed handlers; geometry-only count patches leave text retention reachable.
With size=3 the outer cursor advances six bytes. EXTTEXTOUT's count at payload+4 can come from the next unknown-0xFFFF header; options may select a later optional-rectangle string offset. Subsequent header bytes repeatedly supply large whole-file text spans. Both drawing and VML image relationships reach this decoder before the general image crate's default 512 MiB allocation limit, which therefore cannot bound this earlier retention. The supplied alternating-header proof gives options=3, selecting the optional-rectangle branch and a string start at payload+16.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): WMF variable-length record data is read against the whole input rather than the record's declared slice; declared record progression permits overlapping unbounded amplification.

previousFindings.remediation: Confine every WMF handler, including field, font, string and geometry reads, to a slice limited to its checked declared record extent. Before allocation validate fixed fields, ring/point counts and coordinate arrays, EXTTEXTOUT options/optional rectangle and text count, and TEXTOUT padded string plus trailing coordinates against that slice using checked arithmetic. Refuse inconsistent records before decoding/rasterization/replay and enforce cumulative decoded-text, record and total geometry/work budgets. Keep the already bounded EMF behavior.
