taxonomy.category: Improper link resolution in temporary-file publication

codeEvidence.label: Python writes predictable staging with ordinary open
codeEvidence.explanation: An existing predictable partial symlink is followed and its referent truncated before replace moves the symlink.

codeEvidence.label: Node repeats the predictable nonexclusive staging operation
codeEvidence.explanation: writeFileSync uses default truncating/following semantics and does not exclusively reserve the partial file.

codeEvidence.label: Python --plan operation recording reaches staging
codeEvidence.explanation: A normal non-dry-run plan recording operation invokes _record after reading source.

codeEvidence.label: Node --plan operation recording reaches staging
codeEvidence.explanation: The same supported operation reaches recordPlan in the Node CLI.

rootCause.summary: Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.

previousFindings.remediation: Use exclusive, unpredictable staging owned by a private directory, hold the opened handle through writing, and rename that verified file. Reuse the native publication design or equivalent mkstemp/exclusive wx APIs and never follow existing staging entries.

counterEvidence: Requires write access to the parent plan directory and victim target permissions.
Private plan directories and dry-run avoid the path.
Native Rust publication uses private exclusive UUID staging and does not share this specific defect.
limitations: No attack was executed.
Exact PID discovery and shared-directory permissions are deployment prerequisites.
validation.summary: Verified supported --plan plus operation callers, preview-before-write, and both predictable staging sinks. Preview validates plan semantics, not staging ownership. Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.

rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): The edit/add operation path calls _record after normal plan parsing and document preview. _record resolves the intended final plan but constructs a predictable sibling temporary path using the process ID. Path.write_bytes opens that path with normal truncate/follow semantics rather than exclusive creation or no-follow protection. os.replace happens only after the unintended referent has already been modified.

previousFindings.remediation: Use exclusive, unpredictable staging owned by a private directory, hold the opened handle through writing, and rename that verified file. Reuse the native publication design or equivalent mkstemp/exclusive wx APIs and never follow existing staging entries. Python can reuse native publication; Node needs equivalent secure publication semantics.

sourceAssessmentDifferences.title: Recording plans through binding CLIs can corrupt a symlink target

severity.rationale: The impact is corruption of operator-writable files outside the chosen shared directory. Exploitation requires local directory-entry access, a predictable target/PID and a platform configuration that allows symlink following; trusted private plan directories prevent it. No document-only attack or arbitrary executable payload is established.
severity.changeConditions: Routine privileged recording into attacker-writable directories would increase likelihood and impact; exclusive private staging eliminates this path.

confidence.rationale: Both adapters explicitly derive the predictable path and perform default symlink-following writes; native code and its regression show the intended safe alternative.

sourceAssessmentDifferences.remediation: Use secure exclusive private staging in both binding adapters. Expose/reuse native plan publication from Python and implement equivalent exclusive staging and atomic replacement for Node; never truncate an existing PID-derived partial path.

rootCause.summary: Predictable staging paths are opened with truncating, symlink-following writes instead of exclusive private staging.

previousFindings.title: Python and Node plan recording can overwrite unrelated files through staging symlinks
previousFindings.summary: The Python and Node CLIs write plans through a predictable .<plan>.<PID>.partial pathname using nonexclusive truncating writes. A local actor who can create entries in the plan directory can preplace a symlink there and make the victim overwrite another file it can write, before the intended plan replacement.

severity.rationale: Potentially high file-integrity impact but low likelihood: requires a malicious local actor sharing write access to the selected plan directory, knowledge/prediction of the victim PID and writable target under victim authority. No remote exploit or RCE is established.
severity.changeConditions: Raise if plans routinely live in cross-user writable workspaces or a privileged automation service records plans there; private per-user directories substantially reduce exposure.

confidence.rationale: Both adapter source operations and caller guards inspected; neither exclusively creates staging. Standard Path.write_bytes/fs.writeFileSync following/truncation semantics establish the overwrite. No filesystem reproduction.

codeEvidence.label: Recording promises exclusive staging
codeEvidence.code:
The CLI intentionally grants ambient local authority to explicitly requested
paths. It replaces an output symlink itself, not the link's target. Recording
a plan through a symlink retains its documented local behavior: the link stays
in place and its resolved plan file is atomically replaced. Plan recording
uses exclusive staging but concurrent read/modify/write recordings remain
last-writer-wins, not a serialized append or compare-and-swap.
codeEvidence.explanation: The final plan's intentional symlink semantics are documented separately; they do not authorize following a staging-path link.

rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): The edit/add operation path calls _record after normal plan parsing and document preview. _record resolves the intended final plan but constructs a predictable sibling temporary path using the process ID. Path.write_bytes opens that path with normal truncate/follow semantics rather than exclusive creation or no-follow protection. os.replace happens only after the unintended referent has already been modified.

previousFindings.remediation: Use exclusive, unpredictable staging owned by a private directory, hold the opened handle through writing, and rename that verified file. Reuse the native publication design or equivalent mkstemp/exclusive wx APIs and never follow existing staging entries. Python can reuse native publication; Node needs equivalent secure publication semantics.

validation.method: Preserved already-validated Standard evidence and attack paths; serial semantic remediation-subsumption reduction only, without code inspection, new validation, execution or attack-path analysis
validation.summary:
Verified supported --plan plus operation callers, preview-before-write, and both predictable staging sinks. Preview validates plan semantics, not staging ownership. Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration (preserved Standard static assessment, not reducer verification): Verified edit-with-plan recording entrypoints, successful plan preview, non-dry-run branch, partial-name construction and write/rename in both adapters. The write follows an existing symlink before rename, so later replacement cannot undo referent damage.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): The source selects _record whenever --plan and inline operations are present. Successful preview and dry_run=false reach partial.write_bytes with no prior exclusive allocation or symlink check. On a platform/directory permitting symlink following, a preexisting temporary symlink directs that write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI's account. The subsequent replace moves the symlink over the plan path. This does not require modifying the legitimate plan target itself.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. A precreated internal partial symlink redirects the write before rename. The attacker needs directory-entry rights, not write access to the victim-owned referent.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Python `partial.write_bytes` and Node `fs.writeFileSync` use default creation/truncation behavior after constructing the same predictable name. No code checks the staging object's identity. Preview runs first but does not constrain that file. Native `write_plan` now delegates to secure publication, and a current regression explicitly verifies it does not open the legacy partial symlink.

findings.title: Legacy edit-anchor searches compare long prefixes at every character
findings.summary: Legacy plan resolution searches for an anchor with starts_with at every character position, including its normalized fallback. A repetitive paragraph paired with a long near-matching anchor can force quadratic CPU work before the plan is refused or applied.

severity.rationale: Potential high CPU impact but low likelihood: requires a consumer to resolve a long attacker-influenced legacy plan anchor against a repetitive document. No remote/automatic hostile-plan deployment established.
severity.changeConditions: Effective host isolation and narrower exposure lower impact/likelihood; automatic untrusted workflows increase exposure.

confidence.rationale: Source-backed input-to-operation trace and explicit controls/counterevidence; no application execution or deployment assumption.

codeEvidence.label: Legacy find_range forwards caller anchors
codeEvidence.explanation: Normal plan range resolution reaches locate with the caller's find text.

codeEvidence.label: Exact search compares an anchor at every character
codeEvidence.explanation: Every suffix can repeat the same long prefix comparison.

codeEvidence.label: Normalized fallback repeats the same search
codeEvidence.explanation: Normalization changes representation but does not remove the quadratic search behavior.

rootCause.summary: locate builds hits_of by applying starts_with(needle) to each text suffix. reading_hits repeats the same algorithm after normalization. Long shared prefixes are compared repeatedly with no search-work budget, unlike the KMP-based v2 candidate matcher. An a^N paragraph and a^(N/2)b anchor make each early comparison traverse most of the anchor before failing.

findings.remediation: Use a linear-time substring matcher for exact and normalized legacy anchors, reusing the v2 KMP approach, while preserving overlapping-hit semantics and source-offset mapping. Add explicit cumulative matching-work limits where needed.

counterEvidence: v2 candidate matching uses a linear KMP implementation; this report is limited to the legacy resolver.
Short anchors/ordinary paragraphs are bounded in practice.
Caller-controlled plan text is an additional prerequisite, not automatically supplied by every malicious document.
limitations: No crafted file or application execution.
validation.summary: Independently followed Replace -> find_range4164-4180 -> locate5763-5820 and the normalized fallback79-92. Both search implementations inspect every character suffix; no anchor-length/product-work cap appears in this path. The concrete high-cost case needs influence over both document text and the selected legacy anchor, so likelihood is lower than document-only parser findings.

finding.title: Redaction's leak scan misses confidential text split across DrawingML runs
finding.summary: xml_holds checks individual XML text nodes, then reconstructs split text only for WordprocessingML w:p paragraphs and w:t/w:delText/w:instrText nodes. DrawingML a:p paragraphs and a:t runs in chart or diagram parts are excluded. Consequently, a redaction can remove a body occurrence and pass the final leak check while a duplicate secret remains divided across DrawingML text runs in an unchanged auxiliary part. Neither individual text node contains the entire needle, and no DrawingML joined-text check runs. The supposedly redacted DOCX retains recoverable confidential text in its preserved XML; downstream Office rendering can retain the corresponding chart/diagram text.

severity.rationale: Confidential text survives a documented redaction boundary in an artifact intended to be shared. The demonstrated mixed-plan/split-run path is deterministic, but an unauthorized recipient requires the caller's later report/document sharing.
severity.changeConditions: Impact depends on the sensitivity of the removed content and audience of the report/document; keeping artifacts private avoids disclosure to other actors.

confidence.rationale: Independently verified scanner/report construction, serialized exposure, source preservation and counterevidence; no runtime reproduction was performed.

findings.title: Streaming XML hash repeatedly rescans growing escaped opening tags
findings.summary: HashXmlBuf searches the entire accumulated opening tag for > after every emitted fragment. Escaped attribute values emit one fragment per character; retained custom-namespace paragraph attributes select this fallback hashing path, causing quadratic CPU consumption within admitted XML sizes.

severity.rationale: A supplied document directly induces disproportionate memory/CPU consumption in a victim processing it. Impact is process availability; no remote-service or cross-tenant deployment is inferred.

confidence.rationale: Direct offline source validation establishes caller-controlled input, effective controls and sensitive operation. No triggering input or application code executed.

codeEvidence.label: Every fragment rescans the growing root tag
codeEvidence.explanation: A large escaped attribute is emitted in tiny fragments before any > appears.

codeEvidence.label: Attribute escaping emits one fragment per character
codeEvidence.code:
for c in s.chars() {
        match c {
            '&' => out.push_str("&"),
            '<' => out.push_str("<"),
            '>' => out.push_str(">"),
            '"' => out.push_str("""),
            '\t' => out.push_str("	"),
            '\n' => out.push_str("
"),
            '\r' => out.push_str(""),
            _ => out.push(c),
        }
codeEvidence.explanation: Each escaped ampersand appends five bytes then triggers another whole-tag scan.

codeEvidence.label: Custom namespace selects fallback hashing
codeEvidence.explanation: Retained attributes outside Word/empty namespace cause fast hash to decline.

rootCause.summary: Root-tag buffering repeatedly searches old bytes on every character-sized escaped fragment instead of searching newly appended bytes or signaling tag completion.

findings.remediation: Search only the new fragment for the root-tag terminator or expose explicit tag-completion state from serialization. Preserve linear behavior for escaped values and test large retained custom attributes through public comparison.

counterEvidence: Simple paragraphs fast-hash; custom namespace causes explicit fallback.
One namespace declaration and one permitted attribute stay within count/name/value/start-tag budgets.
SHA1 content keys' nonauthentication role is unrelated to this CPU issue.
Identical input packages shortcut comparison; differing documents reach normal hashing.
limitations: No runtime reproduction or deployment verified.
validation.summary: Parent verified HashXmlBuf append/find (serialize.rs:501-516), character escaping (548-558), retained paragraph attrs (preprocess.rs:306-312), custom-namespace fallback (742-769), block_sha1_from_source fallback (657-679) and comparison block-hash pipeline (comparer/mod.rs:655-667; preprocess.rs:1276-1281). One million escaped ampersands in x:a (~5MB XML) imply~2.5TB cumulative byte searches. Choose differing input packages to avoid identical-input shortcuts.

dataflow.summary: Admitted paragraph x:a -> retained clone -> fast path returns None -> block_sha1 -> HashXmlBuf -> per-character escaped fragment -> repeated full opening-tag find.

impact.rationale: Worker or embedding-process memory/CPU exhaustion.

likelihood.rationale: The affected source consumer is directly reached from ordinary supplied input.

preconditions: Victim compares supplied DOCX against a genuinely different document.

Retain correct hashes for ordinary attributes and for the custom-namespace fallback, including fragments that terminate or span the root opening tag.

findings.title: Nested semantic fields multiply retained instructions and hash work
findings.summary: Field salting copies each instruction into every open semantic field and materializes the full chain again for every atom. Sibling fldChar begin/end markers can create arbitrarily deep field nesting at shallow XML depth, amplifying a modest instruction into gigabytes.

severity.rationale: A supplied document directly induces disproportionate memory/CPU consumption in a victim processing it. Impact is process availability; no remote-service or cross-tenant deployment is inferred.

confidence.rationale: Direct offline source validation establishes caller-controlled input, effective controls and sensitive operation. No triggering input or application code executed.

taxonomy.category: Unbounded allocation and work from semantic field nesting

codeEvidence.label: Each instruction copied into all open semantic fields
codeEvidence.explanation: Sibling field markers can create deep semantic nesting without deep XML.

codeEvidence.label: Every atom materializes full open-code chain
codeEvidence.explanation: Duplicated full instructions are copied and hashed again for every atom.

codeEvidence.label: Body comparison atomizes before LCS shortcuts
codeEvidence.explanation: Both caller-controlled bodies reach unconditional field salting.

codeEvidence.label: Salting unconditional after atom construction
codeEvidence.explanation: Semantic field depth and aggregate instruction bytes are not limited here.

rootCause.summary: Semantic field depth and aggregate instruction/hash-chain work are unbounded; full instruction strings are duplicated across open fields and per-atom chains.

findings.remediation: Bound semantic field depth and total instruction/hash work before copying. Use shared instruction representations and incremental/compositional field hashes instead of materializing every full nested code chain; return a typed refusal when budgets are exceeded.

counterEvidence: Byte-identical and normalized-identical documents bypass atomization; use differing documents.
XML depth counts element ancestry, not sibling field begin/end nesting.

findings.title: Tolerated XML syntax can hide recursive elements from admission
findings.summary: A DOCX author can place nested element text inside an XML comment after an unquoted attribute. Admission counts only shallow quick-xml events, while the permissive DOM parser consumes that attribute differently and recursively interprets the hidden tags. The normal .xml path can therefore exhaust the host stack despite max_xml_depth.

severity.rationale: A small crafted document can reliably cause disproportionate allocation or stack use in a public parser path; impact is process availability, likelihood high when consumed. No remote deployment is assumed.

confidence.rationale: Source establishes the complete relevant branch/control/dataflow. Runtime execution and deployment-specific exposure were not tested.

rootCause.summary: Admission uses quick-xml events and TagPolicy::tolerant, which accepts unquoted attributes, and ignores comments/DTD events for element depth. The downstream parser assumes the first attribute-value character is a quote delimiter even when it is not a quote. It can consume across the start-tag boundary into a comment, then parse comment content as real elements. Its DOCTYPE skip also stops at the first > rather than the end of an internal subset, creating a related interpretation gap.

findings.remediation: Make admission and DOM construction consume the same grammar, reject unsupported DTDs at package admission, parse unquoted values correctly or refuse them, and enforce a hard depth budget inside DOM construction.

counterEvidence: Correctly quoted ordinary XML without DTD/comment interpretation gaps receives the expected depth check.
Standalone checked XML parsing rejects the unquoted route and DTD; the report concerns public package processing using tolerant admission and raw DOM construction.
No external entity resolution, network/file access or entity expansion is claimed.
limitations: No application code or malicious fixture executed; platform/runtime behavior was assessed from source.
validation.summary: For the unquoted/comment route, `<r a=x><!-- x>` followed by nested tags and a comment close is a shallow root/comment sequence to admission; raw parse_element treats the first x as a quote and the x inside the comment as its close. It then reaches the nested tags without recognizing the comment opener it already consumed. No later depth guard exists before recursive parse_element. A DTD internal entity literal containing nested tags similarly falls under ignored DocType events but the raw skip consumes only the first >. These are grammar interpretation issues, not external-entity fetching. Strict validate_xml uses quoted attributes and explicitly refuses DTDs, but rendering's package-admission path does not invoke that strict gate.

findings.summary: A document returned successfully by scrub can retain creator/editor identities, company/custom properties, revision authors, session IDs and people information when valid OPC relationships locate those parts outside conventional filenames or word/. Sharing the supposedly scrubbed output discloses the retained data. Supported relocated stories include content/main.xml and word/main.dat; a conventional prefix or .xml suffix is not semantic part identity.

codeEvidence.label: Conventional metadata filenames are hardcoded

rootCause.summary: `scrub_properties` hardcodes docProps/core.xml, app.xml and custom.xml. `alias_authors` and `remove_rsids` enumerate only word/*.xml, and people cleanup looks up word/people.xml. OPC part identity is relationship/content-type based, so valid relocated parts are skipped. The final check rejects new structural findings, not residual privacy-sensitive fields, and can return those bytes successfully.

finding.remediation: Discover all applicable metadata, people, comments, settings and story parts through relationships and content types. Apply the requested transforms to every discovered part and assert privacy-specific postconditions before returning success.

counterEvidence: Conventional UTF-8 parts at expected paths receive the intended transformations.
Active relocated comments can introduce COMMENT_UNANCHORED after references are removed, causing safe refusal; this finding does not claim successful leakage for that case.
A preexisting orphan-comment case was observed as a secondary possibility, but core/app/custom and author/rsid/people paths establish the primary finding without relying on it.
The module mentions word/ internally; public scrub/Document.scrub privacy promises are broader and no package constraint mandates those filenames.
limitations: No document was generated, shared or opened in Word during review.
validation.summary: Confirmed relocated core/app/custom metadata has no privacy transform or final residual-field check. Main/story parts outside word/ are supported by relationship discovery yet excluded from author/rsid enumeration. These values remain in the output package on successful validity checks.

dataflow.summary: Relationship-selected alternate part -> PartFs preserves bytes -> hardcoded scrub path selection skips it -> validity-only postcheck -> successful output -> recipient reads retained metadata.

impact.why: Confidentiality loss of selected identifying information.

likelihood.why: Requires alternate valid locations and downstream sharing.

reachability.summary: An input document producer controls part names/relationships; ordinary alternate-location documents can also trigger the failure. The recipient gains identifiers the privacy operation promised to remove.

finding.title: Sharing a scrubbed DOCX can retain authors and metadata at valid alternate part paths
finding.summary: `scrub` advertises removing authors and identifying metadata before sharing, but discovers author-bearing parts only under `word/` with `.xml` names and properties only at fixed `docProps` filenames. Valid relationship-selected alternate parts remain unsanitized in the returned package.

severity.rationale: Selected confidential metadata survives a user-invoked sharing workflow; impact and exposure are conditional and limited to identifiers.

confidence.rationale: Parent independently traced actual current source, checked relevant controls and sibling operations; no application code or exploit input was executed.

codeEvidence.label: Scrub processing
codeEvidence.explanation: Relationship-selected main existence is accepted before selected privacy operations run.

codeEvidence.label: Lexical part filter
codeEvidence.explanation: Non-word paths and non-xml extensions are excluded despite supported OPC naming.

codeEvidence.label: Author iteration
codeEvidence.explanation: Alias replacement only visits the filtered names.

codeEvidence.label: Fixed property locations
codeEvidence.explanation: Missing conventional property parts are skipped and alternate targets remain.

codeEvidence.label: Supported alternate main part
codeEvidence.explanation: An existing admission test establishes content/main.xml is an accepted relationship-selected main part.

codeEvidence.label: CLI privacy contract
codeEvidence.code:
/// Remove authors, editing IDs, metadata and comments before sharing.
    #[command(after_help = "Examples:\n  \
        jubarte scrub redline.docx -o out.docx                     everything, alias Author\n  \
        jubarte scrub redline.docx -o out.docx --author-alias Counsel --rsids\n  \
        jubarte scrub redline.docx -o out.docx --comments          comments only")]
codeEvidence.explanation: The user action is advertised as removing identifying data before sharing.

codeEvidence.label: Python removal contract
codeEvidence.explanation: The wrapper promises every selected author and metadata category is removed and forwards options into the native scrubber.

rootCause.summary: `scrub()` opens an OPC package and checks only that its relationship-selected main part exists. `alias_authors()` filters lexical `word/*.xml`; `scrub_properties()` loads conventional constants instead of relationship targets/content types. Absent conventional parts are silently skipped, and validation only rejects newly introduced findings rather than proving identifiers were removed.

finding.remediation: Discover relevant story, people and property parts through relationships/content types rather than conventional filenames or extensions; sanitize the selected semantic categories and fail closed if they cannot be inspected.

counterEvidence: The Rust module describes its narrower word/ implementation, but CLI/Python advertise removal for every author and metadata before sharing.
Text, revision dates and unselected categories intentionally remain; they are outside this finding.
No remote exposure or public repository access is assumed. Input may be nonmalicious and merely use alternate names.
limitations: No runtime reproduction; deployment isolation and externally imposed quotas were not supplied.
validation.summary: Valid DOCX with main part content/main.xml (or word/main.dat), author-bearing revisions and relocated metadata -> PartFs -> lexical scrub selectors skip those parts -> to_zip preserves them -> user shares successful output -> recipient reads original identifiers.

controls: The Rust module describes its narrower word/ implementation, but CLI/Python advertise removal for every author and metadata before sharing.
Text, revision dates and unselected categories intentionally remain; they are outside this finding.
No remote exposure or public repository access is assumed. Input may be nonmalicious and merely use alternate names.

dataflow.summary: Valid DOCX with main part content/main.xml (or word/main.dat), author-bearing revisions and relocated metadata -> PartFs -> lexical scrub selectors skip those parts -> to_zip preserves them -> user shares successful output -> recipient reads original identifiers.

impact.why: Disclosure of reviewer identities, edit-session identifiers and creator/company/custom-property information the caller asked to remove.

likelihood.why: A recipient of an output generated through CLI scrub, Python Document.scrub or WASM scrubDocument can recover selected identifiers when the input uses valid alternate OPC part names; operator publication of the returned document is required.

reachability.summary: A recipient of an output generated through CLI scrub, Python Document.scrub or WASM scrubDocument can recover selected identifiers when the input uses valid alternate OPC part names; operator publication of the returned document is required.
reachability.attacker: Recipient of an intentionally shared, supposedly sanitized output.
preconditions: A recipient of an output generated through CLI scrub, Python Document.scrub or WASM scrubDocument can recover selected identifiers when the input uses valid alternate OPC part names; operator publication of the returned document is required.

attackPath.summary: `scrub` advertises removing authors and identifying metadata before sharing, but discovers author-bearing parts only under `word/` with `.xml` names and properties only at fixed `docProps` filenames. Valid relationship-selected alternate parts remain unsanitized in the returned package.

remediationTests: Use a small deterministic document with extreme semantic values or alternate valid OPC paths and assert controlled refusal or complete selected sanitization before expensive processing.

findings.title: UTF-16 XML can retain confidential text after successful scrub or redaction
findings.summary: Jubarte accepts UTF-16 XML but scrub and leak detection read it as lossy UTF-8. Metadata transforms silently skip it, and redaction postchecks can miss a remaining confidential copy in UTF-16 custom XML while returning successful output.

severity.rationale: The failure defeats an explicit whole-package redaction/privacy postcondition and can disclose confidential text when output is distributed. It requires an accepted UTF-16 copy and a sharing workflow; it does not provide ambient file access.
severity.changeConditions: Encoding-aware fail-closed validation or removal of the retained copy prevents disclosure. Reliance on redaction before public sharing increases impact.

confidence.rationale: Supported admission encoding, mismatched decoder, no-root behavior, extension-based fallback and final redaction consumer were independently traced; unmodified parts are explicitly preserved.

codeEvidence.label: Admission supports BOM-prefixed UTF-16 XML
codeEvidence.explanation: Accepted UTF-16LE/BE parts are transcoded for the input policy, establishing this as supported data.

codeEvidence.explanation: Privacy transforms using part_string receive the wrong representation for accepted UTF-16 XML.

codeEvidence.explanation: XML/.rels go through lossy UTF-8; the UTF-16 raw needle comparison is only used for non-XML members.

codeEvidence.label: Unparsed XML falls back to lossy substring search
codeEvidence.explanation: BOM replacement characters prevent a root, while interleaved NULs prevent an ordinary secret needle from matching.

codeEvidence.label: Untouched parts retain exact bytes
codeEvidence.explanation: Editing the visible story does not rewrite or strip a UTF-16 custom XML copy of the same secret.

codeEvidence.label: Redaction trusts an empty leak result
codeEvidence.explanation: The confidentiality postcondition treats no reported parts as success, so a missed UTF-16 copy avoids REDACTION_LEAK.

rootCause.summary: Admission's `part_text` decodes UTF-16 BOMs, but `PartFs::part_string` and the XML branch of `leaks_within` apply `String::from_utf8_lossy`. A UTF-16 BOM becomes a leading replacement character and the permissive parser returns no root. Scrub skips that part, while `xml_holds` searches a string with interleaved NULs; the raw UTF-16 fallback is excluded for XML members. `check_redactions` trusts the empty result for both clean and redline outputs.

findings.remediation: Use one encoding-aware XML decoder for admission, privacy transformations and leakage checks. Fail closed when an accepted XML part cannot be decoded or parsed for a privacy operation; scan all supported encodings consistently before certifying redaction.

counterEvidence: Archive reads/inflation fail closed, but successful byte retrieval does not establish successful decoding.
The non-XML branch scans raw UTF-16LE needles; legitimate .xml/.rels parts bypass that branch.
UTF-8 entity/text-run handling does not repair the encoding mismatch.
Admission tests at src/admission.rs:1845-1863 explicitly accept UTF-16 custom XML; this is not an unsupported-encoding claim.
limitations: No document was generated, edited or shared at runtime during review.
validation.summary: Confirmed an ordinary ASCII secret in BOM-prefixed UTF-16 XML is not contiguous in the lossy UTF-8 string. The leading BOM decoding prevents a DOM root, so neither XML text scanning nor fallback substring matching finds it. Editing a visible UTF-8 copy leaves custom XML unchanged; prepared output paths call check_redactions at lines 804 and 873.

dataflow.summary: Accepted UTF-16 XML bytes -> untouched package member -> lossy UTF-8 privacy/leak decode -> no DOM root -> NUL-interleaved substring miss -> empty leaks -> successful clean/redline output.

findings.title: Revision settlement performs quadratic paragraph correspondence work
findings.summary: A compact DOCX with many paragraphs and one tracked insertion can force a Cartesian scan of original and settled paragraphs when an ordinary edit/read/template request accepts or rejects revisions. The scan runs even when no paragraph merged, allowing disproportionate CPU use.

severity.rationale: The request crosses a public untrusted-document processing boundary and the source proves quadratic work within ordinary revision settlement. The impact is availability of the invoking worker; settlement must be requested.
severity.changeConditions: Documents processed without settlement skip this path. CPU-limited isolated workers reduce the blast radius.

confidence.rationale: Settlement changed-state, Origin construction and the unconditional nested scan were independently traced. The operation count is structural; elapsed exploit time was not measured.

codeEvidence.label: Revision settlement marks the source changed
codeEvidence.explanation: Accepting/rejecting existing revisions sets flattened and changed, even if only a run-level revision changed.

codeEvidence.label: Changed settlement builds source correspondence
codeEvidence.explanation: Ordinary edit startup invokes Origin for all loaded paragraphs after settlement.

codeEvidence.label: All paragraphs enter fate calculation
codeEvidence.explanation: Both source and settled paragraph collections determine the Cartesian scan dimensions.

codeEvidence.label: Every settled paragraph scans every source fate
codeEvidence.explanation: The loop collects merged members by scanning the complete fates array for each post, including when no merges exist.

rootCause.summary: Any requested revision settlement that changes source bytes invokes `Origin::build`. It computes paragraph fates for the entire document. The final merged-singleton reconciliation loops over every settled paragraph and scans every original fate to collect matching members, instead of grouping merged members once. The loop is unconditional even when the source contains no merged paragraphs.

findings.remediation: Build merged-member counts and singleton source indexes in one pass over fates, keyed by settled paragraph, then inspect only singleton merged groups. Review neighboring repeated scans and enforce an explicit correspondence-work budget.

counterEvidence: Unchanged/no-settlement documents skip Origin construction; the attack includes a revision and requests settlement.
Correct source_sha256 binding does not reduce the work on the bound document.
Admission has byte/depth/entry limits, not a paragraph-correspondence work budget; compact paragraphs fit defaults.
Requested revision modification is authorized; excessive processing cost is the security issue.
limitations: No timing benchmark, crafted DOCX or application execution was performed.
validation.summary: Confirmed one run-level insertion plus a legitimate accept/reject settlement preserves nearly all paragraph counts while setting changed=true. For roughly 100,000 ordinary/empty paragraphs, the loop alone evaluates about ten billion fate comparisons; this is an operation count, not a timing measurement.

dataflow.summary: Document paragraphs + revision -> requested accept/reject settlement -> changed -> Origin::build -> fates -> settled-count times original-count comparisons.

impact.why: Process availability loss through quadratic work.

likelihood.why: The qualifying settlement request unconditionally reaches the Cartesian scan.

reachability.summary: Public v1 apply/preview/check, v2 apply, read-for-edit and template generation share this correspondence consumer when settlement changes bytes; bindings forward those APIs.
reachability.outcome: Disproportionate worker CPU consumption.
preconditions: The operation accepts/rejects at least one revision.

attackPath.summary: Supply a compact DOCX with many empty paragraphs and one tracked run, then request a valid edit, read-for-edit or template workflow that settles that revision.

remediationTests: Exercise many unchanged paragraphs plus one settled run revision and assert correspondence work remains linear.
Cover v1/v2, read-for-edit and template consumers while retaining merged-singleton correctness.

findings.title: Nested Markdown header or footer fields can overflow the conversion stack
findings.summary: An attacker-controlled header/footer scalar can contain thousands of nested short field results. The Markdown story writer recursively materializes each result without a nesting limit, causing stack exhaustion or substantial repeated scanning before DOCX output validation.

severity.rationale: A compact caller-controlled Markdown scalar reaches unbounded recursion in normal conversion. The supported impact is worker availability; crash depth varies with the host.
severity.changeConditions: Depth/work limits or an iterative writer prevent the failure. Isolated conversion workers constrain the blast radius.

confidence.rationale: Parent verified scalar restoration, story writing, matching nested fields, per-instruction cap and unguarded recursive runs calls in current source.

findings.title: Rendering a long paragraph performs quadratic suffix scans
findings.summary: Wrapping computes every remaining token suffix before line breaking, even when the paragraph contains no tabs and does not need suffix widths.

severity.rationale: An untrusted document can cause disproportionate CPU/memory consumption in the processing host. Availability impact is medium and the direct input path has high likelihood; no execution or disclosure is established.
severity.changeConditions: Per-job CPU/memory isolation limits collateral impact; shared long-lived service deployment increases affected availability.

confidence.rationale: Independent static source inspection confirms input parsing, propagation, missing work/allocation bound and reachable sink. Runtime duration/host failure was not measured.

codeEvidence.label: Words and spaces become separate units
codeEvidence.explanation: Whitespace boundaries produce many units from a short repeated-word paragraph.

codeEvidence.label: Every unit scans its whole suffix
codeEvidence.explanation: Without tabs, each suffix scan reaches the end; N units cause N*(N-1)/2 visits before wrapping.

rootCause.summary: Paragraph runs become word/space units. `wrap_runs_segment()` unconditionally builds `tails` by summing `units[i+1..]` for every i, stopping only at tabs. A tab-free paragraph therefore pays quadratic work for widths that will never be used.

findings.remediation: Compute suffix widths in a single reverse pass with resets at tab boundaries, or skip suffix work for tab-free segments.

counterEvidence: Admission bounds source ZIP/XML size, nesting and entries, and the policy recommends host process limits. These do not bound this generated work.
limitations: No application execution or vulnerability-triggering runtime test was performed.
validation.summary: Checked token splitting, unit construction and wrapping dispatch. Ordinary repeated words separated by single spaces form linearly many units, no explicit line breaks split the segment, and every suffix reaches the end. Byte budgets allow far more units than a practical quadratic scan can process.

finding.title: Scanning deeply nested package XML for leaks can abort the calling process
finding.summary: The public `scrub::leaks()` scanner inflates XML parts under byte budgets but passes them to the permissive recursive DOM parser without enforcing XML depth. A compact package containing sufficiently nested XML can exhaust the stack and abort the caller instead of returning the scanner's documented fail-closed finding.

severity.rationale: A document supplier can trigger unbounded recursion through the public byte-taking leak-scanning API, affecting process availability. No memory-corruption or remote-service claim is made. Normal edit call paths may already admit inputs, and isolated workers constrain impact.
severity.changeConditions: An upload scanning service exposing this public API without worker isolation increases impact; guaranteed pre-admission at all callers would reduce reachability but would not enforce the public API's own boundary.

confidence.rationale: Static source directly shows public entry, only ZIP/byte admission, raw XML parser invocation, and recursive parse_element call with work after recursion. No dynamic stack-overflow test was run.

taxonomy.category: Uncontrolled recursion / missing XML depth admission

codeEvidence.label: Public scanner accepts raw package bytes
codeEvidence.explanation: `leaks` forwards arbitrary package bytes with the comparison limits. `leaks_within` applies preindex_budget and opens the archive, but does not call the full XML admission gate.

codeEvidence.label: Byte limits are followed by unchecked XML scan
codeEvidence.explanation: After bounded inflation, every .xml/.rels part is passed to xml_holds without applying the max_xml_depth field or checked parser.

codeEvidence.label: Leak scan calls permissive DOM construction
codeEvidence.explanation: xml_holds invokes parse_xdocument directly; the selected API deliberately does not enforce input policy. A malformed/deep input is parsed before the scanner can report any result.

codeEvidence.label: Nesting consumes one Rust stack frame per element
codeEvidence.explanation: Nested elements recursively invoke parse_element, and DOM mutation follows the call. No local depth bound or iterative work stack constrains recursion.

rootCause.summary: The leak scanner confuses ZIP inflation budgeting with XML policy admission. It accepts raw document bytes at a public API but invokes the unchecked recursive parser on each XML part, bypassing the depth limit carried in InputLimits and the checked parser's intended gate.

finding.remediation: Before constructing the DOM, enforce the active XML depth/tag policy and return a leak finding on validation failure, preserving the scanner's fail-closed semantics. Alternatively use bounded iterative XML scanning, with explicit handling of malformed XML rather than unsafe recursive fallback.

counterEvidence: The public raw parser itself documents caller responsibility and is not independently reported as unsafe.
Ordinary edit redaction paths can receive already-admitted documents; this finding relies on direct use of the public scrub::leaks byte API.
ZIP structural validation and inflation budgets remain effective, but deep XML fits comfortably below them.
A host subprocess can limit the blast radius; it does not make stack exhaustion a returned leak finding.
limitations: No application execution, triggering fixture or dynamic stack-depth measurement.
No externally exposed leak-scanning service or direct Python/WASM wrapper was established.
validation.summary: Read the complete scrub module, the public raw-versus-checked parser contract and recursive parse branch. Full admission's XML depth scan is not called on this path; preindex_budget and tally_inflated bound container bytes but not nesting. A nonempty search needle reaches XML parsing even when the needle is absent.

dataflow.summary: scrub::leaks(bytes, needle) → leaks_within → bounded entry inflation → xml_holds → parse_xdocument → recursive parse_element.

reachability.summary: The public Rust library boundary accepts the entire untrusted package. No pre-admission obligation is stated by leaks; its documented failure mode is a returned finding for unscannable input. The attacker controls nesting, not the caller's environment.
reachability.attacker: Supplier of package bytes consumed by the public leak scanner
preconditions: Host calls public scrub::leaks directly on supplier bytes with nonempty needle.
XML depth exceeds available process stack and is not pre-admitted by host.

attackPath.summary: A caller uses the public leak scanner on supplier-controlled package bytes and a nonempty needle; an XML part with excessive nesting enters unchecked recursive DOM construction and can terminate the process.

remediationTests: Integration test a deeply nested XML part in an otherwise small package; scanner returns a finding without process termination.
Verify active max_xml_depth is enforced and exact-boundary input still scans.
Keep unreadable-entry and decoded/split-text leak checks fail closed.

findings.summary: An embedded TrueType font with at least 32768 retained directory records reaches a u16 doubling loop while its PDF subset is written. Normal release arithmetic wraps the loop state to zero and never terminates; overflow-checked builds panic.

severity.rationale: A document provider can supply a small font directory with repeated allowed tags and make normal PDF conversion hang or fail. Process availability is the established impact; host CPU limits contain it.

codeEvidence.label: u16 doubling overflows
codeEvidence.explanation: For n>=32768 the next doubling overflows u16; release arithmetic reaches pow=0 and loops forever, while checked arithmetic panics.

rootCause.summary: subset_keep_gids retains every allowed table record without tag deduplication or a semantic table-count maximum. write_sfnt computes the largest power of two using u16 multiplication; at pow=32768, doubling wraps to zero in release and the comparison stays true indefinitely.

findings.title: HTML selector groups multiply CSS values into excessive memory
findings.summary: A DOCX HTML altChunk can combine one large CSS property value with thousands of grouped selectors. The importer deep-copies the complete property map into each selector, consuming gigabytes even if none of the rules are used. A supplied framing uses 4096 distinct selectors and one 1 MiB value for about 4 GiB of retained value storage, excluding overhead; this is a static estimate. Additional supplied static framing: 10000 distinct short selectors sharing a 1 MiB property imply about 10 GiB of retained values from approximately 1.1 MiB HTML; this is not a memory measurement.

severity.rationale: A document sender directly controls both amplification factors in an admitted HTML part, making process memory exhaustion likely for a crafted document. No broader host compromise is inferred.
severity.changeConditions: Sharing immutable declaration storage and enforcing aggregate rule/value budgets removes the amplification.

confidence.rationale: HashMap<String,String> cloning occurs once per attacker-controlled selector before content use; ownership and lifetime are explicit in the full importer.

rootCause.summary: parse_css stores an owned String per declaration, then props.clone deep-copies every value for each selector in the group. findings.title: Crafted MATH metrics can expand an equation into excessive glyphs
findings.summary: A document with a crafted embedded math font can make inline fractions increase font size instead of reducing it. An enclosing stretchy delimiter then computes a huge extender count and stores one glyph per repetition, exhausting rendering resources despite shallow XML nesting. The assigned radical variant supplies finite arithmetic: unitsPerEm=1000, leaf yMax=1000, scriptPercentScaleDown=10000 (factor 100), ten nested inline numerator fractions at 12 pt, and one radical extender with fullAdvance=1 and zero overlap. The derived target/advance exceeds 1e23 and saturates to usize::MAX before the glyph loop. This is a supplied static construction, with no crafted-font acceptance or runtime demonstration.

severity.rationale: Availability impact is bounded to the document-processing host. Exploitation requires a valid crafted TrueType MATH font with selected family/glyph/assembly mappings and matching OMML; this specialized prerequisite lowers likelihood. Host limits can contain failure.
severity.changeConditions: A verified minimal font/OMML reproduction would raise confidence and likelihood; semantic metric and cumulative glyph budgets remove the expansion.

confidence.rationale: Source traces document font selection, unrestricted script metrics, geometric multiplication and uncapped assembly allocation; a complete crafted font/OMML pair was not generated or executed.

rootCause.summary: The renderer trusts MATH scale and assembly metrics after structural font parsing. A script percentage above100 increases child size on each inline fraction. Delimiter height derives from the expanded geometry, and assemble converts target/advance into an unchecked repetition count, appending a glyph for each repetition. In the additional radical path, body.ascent+body.descent+gap+rule controls stretch_glyph. Embedded-first family resolution lets a parseable glyf Cambria Math face provide the MATH constants and assembly. Ten inline fraction nests stay below MAX_DEPTH64; fullAdvance=1 at the outer 12-pt size and upem1000 gives .012-pt advance above zero overlap. Finite amplified geometry therefore reaches the same unchecked assembly count without depending on floating infinity. The prior signed-i16 scale correction remains: factor100 is within the reported maximum327.67.

findings.remediation: Validate MATH scale percentages and metrics against supported finite ranges; reject extreme geometry and enforce a cumulative assembly-glyph budget before converting ratios to counts or allocating. Enforce hard per-assembly repetition caps as well as aggregate glyph bounds before floating-point-to-usize casts, and cover both unmarked radicals and delimiters with small positive extender advance above overlap.

previousFindings.title: Crafted MATH metrics can expand an equation into excessive glyphs
previousFindings.summary: A document with a crafted embedded math font can make inline fractions increase font size instead of reducing it. An enclosing stretchy delimiter then computes a huge extender count and stores one glyph per repetition, exhausting rendering resources despite shallow XML nesting.

severity.rationale: Availability impact is bounded to the document-processing host. Exploitation requires a valid crafted TrueType MATH font with selected family/glyph/assembly mappings and matching OMML; this specialized prerequisite lowers likelihood. Host limits can contain failure.
severity.changeConditions: A verified minimal font/OMML reproduction would raise confidence and likelihood; semantic metric and cumulative glyph budgets remove the expansion.

confidence.rationale: Source traces document font selection, unrestricted script metrics, geometric multiplication and uncapped assembly allocation; a complete crafted font/OMML pair was not generated or executed.

rootCause.summary: The renderer trusts MATH scale and assembly metrics after structural font parsing. A script percentage above100 increases child size on each inline fraction. Delimiter height derives from the expanded geometry, and assemble converts target/advance into an unchecked repetition count, appending a glyph for each repetition.

previousFindings.remediation: Validate MATH scale percentages and metrics against supported finite ranges; reject extreme geometry and enforce a cumulative assembly-glyph budget before converting ratios to counts or allocating.

counterEvidence: XML and math recursion have explicit depth bounds; they do not bound multiplicative geometry or derived glyph counts.
The attack needs parseable glyf/MATH tables, visible glyph metrics, and the selected family rather than any arbitrary font bytes.
Ordinary font MATH scale values reduce scripts and do not trigger the amplification.
limitations: Full crafted-font validity, selected mappings and exploit reliability were not dynamically demonstrated.
validation.summary: The font parser accepts and retains MATH constants; script_percent_scale_down is signed i16 in matching ttf-parser0.25.1 (math.rs:176-179), so the maximum positive factor is327.67, correcting the worker's provisional u16 assumption. A few nested inline fractions remain below MAX_DEPTH64 while multiplying geometry. A valid delimiter assembly with a small positive extender advance above overlap makes the target/advance ratio enormous. No bound or finite-output refusal precedes the glyph loop. Existing embedded math families are retained instead of installed replacement.

findings.title: Release script exposes the PyPI publishing token in process arguments
findings.summary: The release operator exports UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN, which preflight checks without printing. Step 11 then expands that credential into `uv publish --token "$UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN" dist/pypi/*`. The spawned uv process therefore contains the token in argv, exposing it through process listings or command-line telemetry on hosts permitting those observations. Disclosure of a PyPI publishing credential. An observer could use the captured token to publish packages within its granted scope until expiration or revocation. Its exact scope and lifetime are not established by the source. The assigned audit leaves uv argument-scrubbing timing and host process permissions unverified, yielding a medium-confidence assessment retained alongside the established high-confidence source-flow assessment.

severity.rationale: A publish token may allow high-impact package publication, but exploitation requires a local process observer on a release host during uv publishing. Platform process visibility and token scope are unknown; constrained local likelihood is low.
severity.changeConditions: Severity increases on shared release hosts exposing cross-user argv or retaining command-line telemetry; host process-visibility restrictions reduce exposure.

confidence.rationale: Current script directly expands the documented token into child arguments; no actual credential value or deployment visibility was inspected.

codeEvidence.label: Publish token in argv
codeEvidence.code:
python3 scripts/check_release_artifacts.py dist/pypi --version "$VER" \
      || die "wheel set incomplete; see scripts/check_release_artifacts.py"
  fi
  uv publish --token "$UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN" dist/pypi/*
  step "uv publish done"
codeEvidence.explanation: Shell expansion copies the secret reference's runtime value into uv argv.

codeEvidence.label: Release preflight identifies private publishing token
codeEvidence.code:
[ -s "$HOME/.cargo/credentials.toml" ] || [ -s "$HOME/.cargo/credentials" ] \
  || [ -n "${CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN:-}" ] \
  || die "no crates.io credentials — run \`cargo login\`"
npm whoami >/dev/null 2>&1 || die "not logged in to npm — run \`npm login\`"
gh auth status >/dev/null 2>&1 || die "gh not authenticated — run \`gh auth login\`"
[ -n "${UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN:-}" ] \
  || die "UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN not set — a pypi-… API token for \`uv publish\`"
step "tools + credentials OK"
codeEvidence.explanation: The operator supplies a PyPI API token through environment; no literal secret is committed.

codeEvidence.label: Reusable token copied into command line
codeEvidence.code:
# One wheel per README platform row (seven). A release.yml run that lost
    # a wheel job must not ship a partial set under a final version.
    python3 scripts/check_release_artifacts.py dist/pypi --version "$VER" \
      || die "wheel set incomplete; see scripts/check_release_artifacts.py"
  fi
  uv publish --token "$UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN" dist/pypi/*
  step "uv publish done"
fi
codeEvidence.explanation: Shell expansion places the private token in uv process argv, where host process inspection may expose it beyond the operator.

rootCause.summary:
The exported publishing credential is redundantly passed as a command-line argument.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: Release preflight requires a private PyPI token in `UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN`. The later publication command expands that value into a positional process argument rather than leaving the tool to consume its environment credential. On hosts that allow other local accounts to inspect command lines, argv crosses a broader visibility boundary than the releasing account's private environment.

findings.remediation: Remove the --token argument and let uv obtain the already exported UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN through its environment-variable credential mechanism. Keep credential values out of process arguments and release logs.

The token already resides in the release process environment, but argv can be visible to principals who cannot read that protected environment.
No embedded token; no shell tracing or deliberate logging.
Restricted process visibility can prevent attack.
Live validity and scope not tested.

counterEvidence: The script does not print the token explicitly or enable shell tracing.
Observation requires process-command-line visibility during publishing; hosts restricting that visibility reduce exposure.
The token already resides in the release process environment, but argv can be visible to principals who cannot read that protected environment.
limitations: No token value read, used or validated.
Actual token privileges/lifetime and release-host process visibility unknown.
validation.summary: Retained as conditional local credential disclosure, calibrated low from baseline medium because it requires cross-user/telemetry argument visibility on the release host.

dataflow.summary: The release operator exports UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN, which preflight checks without printing. Step 11 then expands that credential into `uv publish --token "$UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN" dist/pypi/*`. The spawned uv process therefore contains the token in argv, exposing it through process listings or command-line telemetry on hosts permitting those observations.

impact.rationale: Disclosure of a PyPI publishing credential. An observer could use the captured token to publish packages within its granted scope until expiration or revocation. Its exact scope and lifetime are not established by the source.

likelihood.rationale: Local host/process observer prerequisite during a privileged publication workflow.

reachability.summary: A local user or process-monitoring principal able to inspect other users' process arguments on the release host, without access to the releaser's protected credential storage or process environment.
preconditions: Maintainer runs the publishing step with UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN exported.
Attacker can observe child command lines without already having token/environment access.

remediationTests: Use a deterministic command-builder test with a dummy token to assert argv never contains credential material while credential injection remains environment-based.

findings.title: Reference metadata stamping builds oversized ZIP indexes before refusal
findings.summary: Pass a reference DOCX/ZIP with far more than 10000 entries to `docx_stamp` or `markdown_stamp`. The helper constructs the ZIP index and allocates,traverses and sorts archive-wide extent metadata before checking the entry cap,so an otherwise rejected reference can consume substantial CPU and memory first.

severity.rationale: Untrusted reference bytes reach unbounded archive indexing in public APIs and Markdown CLI conversion before budget refusal. Impact is process/browser-worker availability and depends on supplied archive size and host limits; no measured threshold or live service compromise is claimed.
severity.changeConditions: Enforced compressed-input limits and isolated resource-limited workers reduce impact; long-lived/concurrent metadata processing increases operational risk.

confidence.rationale: Call ordering and archive-sized allocation/traversal are direct source,contrasted with the normal preindex gate. Actual resource amplification was not measured.

taxonomy.category: Resource limits applied after expensive ZIP parsing

rootCause.summary: Public stamp exports and Markdown conversion ask creator_created for reference attribution. That helper directly uses Package::open,whose first operation is opc::open_archive. The shared opener constructs the ZIP index and runs zip_defects; its extent vector,name copies and sort scale with archive.len(). Only after that work does Package::check_limits reject more than 10000 entries. Unlike PartFs::read_package,this path never calls preindex_budget first.

findings.remediation: Apply a documented compressed-input and declared-entry preindex budget before opening metadata ZIPs,or enforce it centrally in Package::open. Preserve best-effort absent-metadata behavior only after a cheap bounded refusal.

counterEvidence: check_limits eventually rejects excess entries.
ZIP structural consistency remains active.
Individual inflation has a separate 200MiB cap and XML tag/depth policy remains; those do not prevent preindex work.
Ordinary docx_to_markdown uses PartFs::open_within first; this does not establish its same bypass.
limitations: No malicious archive generated/executed; exhaustion threshold unmeasured.
The intentional metadata member-size difference is not a separate reported finding.
validation.summary: Verified direct Rust/Python/WASM exports and native/Python/Node Markdown CLI reference stamping. findings.title: Repeated compressed-image references can exhaust renderer memory
findings.summary: A DOCX can reference one highly compressible embedded image many times. Conversion independently decodes and retains an owned pixel buffer per reference, then clones buffers into page operations. Package byte limits and per-page pixel limits do not bound this aggregate decoded memory.

severity.rationale: A modest document can exhaust the rendering process; wider service impact depends on a downstream deployment and isolation.

confidence.rationale: Parent source trace confirms independent decode inside the reference loop, owned retained buffers and later cloning; allocation arithmetic does not require an observed deployment.

codeEvidence.label: Every drawing decodes its media independently
codeEvidence.explanation: Each attacker-controlled blip reference resolves the same part and independently calls decode_image.

codeEvidence.label: Decoded samples retained per image
codeEvidence.code:
out.push(LaidImage {
                        w: w + inset[0] + inset[2],
                        h: h + inset[1] + inset[3],
                        kind,
codeEvidence.explanation: A separate owned ImageKind is pushed per reference and remains in the collected layout images.

codeEvidence.label: Intrinsic raster becomes owned RGB samples
codeEvidence.explanation: Image decoding allocates at intrinsic dimensions, then returns owned RGB/alpha vectors without any shared conversion-wide budget.

codeEvidence.label: Layout clones samples into page operations
codeEvidence.code:
ImageKind::Rgb {
                width,
                height,
                bytes,
                alpha,
            } => self.current().ops.push(Op::Rgb {
                x,
                y,
                dw,
                dh,
                width: *width,
                height: *height,
                bytes: bytes.clone(),
                alpha: alpha.clone(),
codeEvidence.explanation: Each painted image clones the already-retained sample vectors into the display list, before PDF interning.

rootCause.summary: Image collection visits each drawing/blip independently, resolves its part and calls `decode_image()`. Non-JPEG raster decoding returns owned intrinsic-size RGB/alpha vectors. Each reference retains that ImageKind in a LaidImage; painting clones the vectors again into page operations. No shared decoded cache or conversion-wide pixel/byte accounting exists on this path, so repeated references amplify one compressed part without increasing archive inflation correspondingly.

findings.remediation: Apply a conversion-wide decoded-pixel/byte budget before decoding or retaining media, cache decoded parts by source and transformation, and use shared immutable samples in layout/display operations. Count transformed and temporary buffers against the same budget.

counterEvidence: Per-decode dependency limits constrain one image, not aggregate retained samples.
Output page raster cap at src/convert/raster.rs:26-42 applies after layout and does not count intrinsic image buffers.
PDF image interning at src/convert/pdf.rs:506-566 happens after collection/display-list allocation.
Package admission bounds original part bytes.
limitations: No high-memory document was executed.
validation.summary: Parent verified the loop, decoder and display-list copy. One 4096x4096 RGB buffer is 50,331,648 bytes; 100 references retain about 4.7 GiB before later copies. Small authored extents avoid large output pages without reducing intrinsic buffers.

dataflow.summary: Repeated blips -> repeated package-part copies -> independent intrinsic raster decode -> separate LaidImage buffers -> cloned page Op::Rgb samples.

reachability.summary: Shared public rendering/layout conversion automatically collects images; no privileged option or remote deployment is required for the library boundary.

attackPath.summary: Embed one compressible 4096x4096 PNG, reference it in many small drawings, and induce PDF/PNG or layout-report conversion.

remediationTests: Assert repeated references share decoded sample storage and remain under an aggregate budget.
Refuse a compressed image set exceeding total decoded limits before retaining copies; cover transforms and alpha intermediates.

findings.title: Predictable plan and font-cache staging paths follow local symlinks
findings.summary: The Python and npm CLIs record edit plans through .<plan-name>.<pid>.partial using ordinary truncating writes. A different local user able to create entries in the plan directory can preplant that name as a symlink to another file writable by the victim; the write truncates and replaces the referent's contents before the rename. The native CLI uses exclusive private staging and does not share this failure. The native font-index writer has the same mechanism when a trusted operator configures its cache parent as a directory writable by another principal (JUBARTE_FONT_INDEX or shared user-font location). Its default per-user cache does not establish that prerequisite.

severity.rationale: This is a conditional local integrity issue requiring a shared attacker-writable plan directory and prediction or observation of the CLI PID. It can overwrite unrelated files with the validated JSON plan using victim privileges; remote reachability and code execution are not established.
severity.changeConditions: Private plan directories remove the attacker prerequisite; use by a more privileged victim in a shared writable directory increases impact.

confidence.rationale: Direct source shows predictable PID names and symlink-following truncating Path.write_bytes/fs.writeFileSync calls. No runtime exploit was executed.

taxonomy.category: Symlink following in temporary file creation

codeEvidence.label: Python predictable symlink-following partial write
codeEvidence.code:
target = Path(os.path.realpath(plan))
        partial = target.with_name(f".{target.name}.{os.getpid()}.partial")
        try:
            partial.write_bytes(recorded["json"].encode("utf-8"))
            os.replace(partial, target)
codeEvidence.explanation: Realpath resolves the plan, not its newly derived partial sibling. write_bytes opens and truncates an existing symlink referent.

codeEvidence.label: npm predictable partial file write
codeEvidence.explanation: Default writeFileSync opens the existing path with truncation and follows symlinks; rename happens after unrelated referent damage.

codeEvidence.label: Native recording uses exclusive publication
codeEvidence.explanation: The corresponding native writer avoids the legacy partial helper, and publication.rs:472-505 creates a private UUID directory and a create_new file.

codeEvidence.label: Font index uses a predictable truncating temporary write
codeEvidence.explanation: A preplanted temporary-path symlink redirects fs::write before the rename. This requires a cache parent writable by a distinct attacker; default private per-user cache is counterevidence.

rootCause.summary: Two host CLI writers construct predictable temporary filenames and open them with truncation instead of exclusively creating private staging files. The same predictable, nonexclusive pattern occurs in the native persistent font index.

findings.remediation: Route Python recording through the existing native exclusive publication function. For npm, exclusively create a randomly named private staging directory/file in the plan parent, write and verify through a held descriptor, then atomically rename. Refuse existing staging names and avoid following links. Apply exclusive private staging to FontIndex::save as well, and keep shared cache storage segregated by OS principal.

counterEvidence: Victim chooses the plan path and no remote service is established.
Private per-user directories prevent another principal from planting the partial name.
Plan generation and preview validate document operations, but neither checks the staging inode.
Default font-cache parent is per-user; a shared configured parent is an explicit extra prerequisite, and same-user self-only control is not an escalation.
limitations: Requires shared writable directory and a different principal who can precreate the predictable name.
The overwritten data is valid plan JSON, not arbitrary binary payload; no execution outcome established.
validation.summary: Parent verified both record entrypaths, preview/dry-run gates, realpath handling, default file-write semantics, and native sibling counterevidence. A pre-existing partial symlink is not checked or opened exclusively. Parent verified installed_family_faces/cjk_family_faces -> indexed_faces -> record -> save; index path is configuration/per-user derived. Font cache is conditionally affected only if a different principal can create its temporary sibling.

dataflow.summary: Victim edit/add recording -> validated JSON -> predictable partial path -> preplanted symlink -> truncating write to outside referent -> rename of symlink into plan path. Native sibling: rendering font lookup -> cache miss -> index.record/save -> predictable .tsv.<pid>.tmp -> victim-privileged fs::write -> rename.

likelihood.rationale: Local shared-directory and PID timing prerequisites.

findings.title: Document font names trigger quadratic persistent index rewrites
findings.summary: Many distinct unknown font names in a DOCX cause the native renderer to record each miss and rewrite the entire growing font index separately. A document supplier can force quadratic CPU/disk work and grow persistent state across conversions without controlling host configuration.

severity.rationale: High worker availability impact from repeated growing-index work, with medium deployment-dependent likelihood; writable default native persistence is required for disk growth.
severity.changeConditions: Disable persistence with JUBARTE_FONT_INDEX=off or isolate per-document quotas to reduce impact; exposed long-lived native renderers with writable shared index face higher risk.

confidence.rationale: Parent traced all-family resolution, missing-family recording and whole-index rewrite; practical runtime threshold was not measured.

codeEvidence.label: Every font-table family triggers resolution
codeEvidence.explanation: Every font-table family triggers resolution; misses remain distinct and each save reads/merges/formats all prior entries.

codeEvidence.explanation: Uncached empty results are recorded; misses remain distinct and each save reads/merges/formats all prior entries.

codeEvidence.explanation: Default native persistence location and disable setting; misses remain distinct and each save reads/merges/formats all prior entries.

rootCause.summary: Document-controlled font-family misses are persisted one at a time with an unbounded whole-index read/merge/sort/write, without batching, eviction or aggregate work/state limits.

findings.remediation: Batch font-index persistence once per conversion, bound/evict recorded unknown names and total index size, limit family-resolution work, and avoid rescanning/reformatting the entire index for each miss.

counterEvidence: Exact repeated names hit cache; attack requires fresh distinct noncatalogue names.
Empty/off JUBARTE_FONT_INDEX disables persistence, and an unwritable location prevents successful disk growth.
Input XML byte limits bound one document but not quadratic work over its distinct names or persistent cross-document cache size.
No arbitrary host path control or filesystem disclosure is asserted.
limitations: No timing, disk-volume or memory measurements, and actual deployment/index permissions unknown.
validation.summary: Parent independently verified font_table rows are eagerly visited (3427-3432), cached_faces stores distinct misses (3042-3055), installed_family_faces uses a family-specific key (2258-2275), indexed_faces records even empty results (3236-3247), and record/save rewrites all accumulated entries (3192-3227). Format sorts the whole index at 3264-3311.

dataflow.summary: DOCX font table -> each unknown family -> cached_faces/installed_family_faces -> indexed_faces miss -> FontIndex::record -> save parses/merges/sorts/rewrites whole growing index -> quadratic aggregate I/O/CPU and persistent growth.

impact.rationale: Worker availability degradation from aggregate quadratic CPU/I/O; persistent state makes later loads larger.

likelihood.rationale: Default native path is proven, but service exposure and disk permissions are unspecified.

reachability.summary: Default native render setup calls add_installed_faces for every font-table entry, including unused families. The font index defaults beside the platform user font directory and is created when possible.
reachability.attacker: Supplier of documents rendered by a native process
preconditions: Victim renders supplied DOCX via native font resolution.
Enabled writable native index for persistent disk effects; distinct missing names avoid cache hits.

remediationTests: With an in-memory fake index backend, verify many unique misses cause bounded writes per conversion and enforce family/index-size limits; retain intentional miss caching semantics.
